0.title: Ecclesiastes: Fear God and Keep His Commandments
0.overview:
Ecclesiastes is one of the most honest books in the Bible about life in a fallen world. It asks the questions most people think in the middle of the night and rarely say aloud. What is the point of all this work? Why do the wicked prosper and the righteous die young? Why does every pleasure fade? What happens when we die? It does not hurry past these questions with easy answers. It makes the reader feel their full weight, and then it points him to God.

The speaker is called the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem (1:1). The ESV's footnote gives his Hebrew title, Qoheleth, which may also be rendered "Convener" or "Collector": one who gathers people to listen and gathers sayings to teach them (12:9). The description fits Solomon, the wisest and richest king Israel ever had. That is part of the book's force. If anyone could have made life work on its own terms, it was he.

Two phrases run through the book. The first is under the sun, which appears twenty-eight times in the ESV. It is the Preacher's vantage point: life as anyone can observe it, from the level of the world. The second is vanity. The ESV notes that the Hebrew word, hebel, means a "mist", a "vapor" or a "mere breath", and that it appears five times in 1:2 and in twenty-nine other verses. The book's verdict, All is vanity (1:2), does not first mean that life is worthless. It means that everything under the sun is breath: real, and impossible to hold.

So the book's great question is What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun? (1:3). The Preacher tests pleasure, achievement, wealth and wisdom, and finds that none of them can outlast death (2:1-17). He sees oppression with no comforter (4:1), money that never satisfies (5:10), wealth without the power to enjoy it (6:2), and justice that seems never to come (8:14). Under the sun alone, there is no final gain.

But two other threads run through the book, and they are its heart. The first is joy. Again and again the Preacher says there is nothing better than to eat, drink and find enjoyment in one's work, because This also, I saw, is from the hand of God (2:24; see also 3:12-13, 22; 5:18-20; 8:15; 9:7-10; 11:7-10). What cannot be seized from the world can be received from God. The second is the fear of God (3:14; 5:7; 7:18; 8:12-13), which becomes the book's final word: Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man (12:13). It is striking that the book never once uses the covenant name LORD in the ESV. It speaks of God, forty-one times: the Creator whom every person, whatever he believes, must reckon with.

The book is also framed by another voice. Someone speaks about the Preacher (says the Preacher, 1:2; 7:27; 12:8) and at the end commends his words and draws the conclusion (12:9-14). The Preacher's words are given by one Shepherd (12:11). So the hard sayings are not to be read as the last word on their own, but as part of a carefully crafted book that leads the reader through honest despair to the fear of God.

The New Testament shows where Ecclesiastes leads. Paul says that creation was indeed subjected to futility, but in hope (Rom 8:20). The Preacher asked what gain there is in toil; after the resurrection Paul could say, in the Lord your labor is not in vain (1 Cor 15:58). The Preacher asked, Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward? (3:21); Christ abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel (2 Tim 1:10). The wisest son of David asked the questions, and Jesus said, something greater than Solomon is here (Matt 12:42). He is the one Shepherd, who said, I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11).

This commentary takes the book chapter by chapter. Chapters 1, 2, 3 and 12, which set out the question and the conclusion, are given more room; the rest are taken a few verses at a time. Every quotation of the ESV has been checked against the ESV text, and every note about the Hebrew rests on the ESV's own footnotes.

1.title: Vanity of Vanities: What Does Man Gain?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Verdict and the Endless Round
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem (v. 1). His verdict comes first: Vanity of vanities, All is vanity (v. 2), and his question second: What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun? (v. 3). Generations, sun, wind and streams all move and never arrive (vv. 4-7). Eye and ear are never satisfied (v. 8), there is nothing new under the sun (v. 9), and no one is remembered (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: Life seen only from under the sun is motion without arrival, and the book makes us feel that before it shows us any way out.

verseByVerse.quote: The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem.

The book opens with a title rather than a name. The ESV calls the speaker the Preacher, and its footnote gives the Hebrew word, Qoheleth, with two other possible renderings: "Convener" or "Collector". He is someone who gathers: he gathers people to listen, and he gathers sayings, weighing and studying and arranging many proverbs with great care (12:9). The word "Preacher" catches the first sense well. This is a man speaking to an assembly about the most serious questions a human being can ask.

He is the son of David, king in Jerusalem. The book never names Solomon, and it may be that it is not meant to be read as his signature so much as in his voice. But the description fits only one son of David who reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel (v. 12), the king of whom it is written, God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding beyond measure (1 Kgs 4:29). That is the point. The man about to say that everything under the sun is vanity is not a failure grumbling in a corner. He is the richest, wisest, most successful man of his age. If anyone could have made life under the sun work, it was he.

And the New Testament puts that king in his place. Something greater than Solomon is here, Jesus said (Matt 12:42). Read the whole book with that sentence in mind: the wisest son of David asks the question, and the greater Son of David is the answer.

verseByVerse.quote: Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher, vanity of vanities! All is vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher, vanity of vanities! All is vanity.

Before he offers a single argument, the Preacher gives his verdict. And he says it as loudly as it can be said. Vanity of vanities is built like "king of kings" or "holy of holies": vanity at its utmost, and he says it twice.

The ESV's footnote on this verse is the key to the whole book. The word translated vanity is hebel, and it refers concretely to a "mist", a "vapor", or a "mere breath", and metaphorically to something fleeting or elusive. It appears five times in this one verse and in twenty-nine other verses of the book. So when the Preacher says All is vanity, he is not first saying that everything is worthless. He is saying that everything is breath. It is real, as your breath on a cold morning is real, and you can see it. But try to grasp it and hold it, and your hand closes on nothing.

That is a more precise and more painful diagnosis than "life is pointless". Work is breath. Pleasure is breath. Wisdom, wealth, reputation and youth are breath. None of them can bear the weight of a human soul that leans its whole life on them. James uses the same picture for life itself: For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes (Jas 4:14).

Notice also that says the Preacher is spoken about him, not by him. Someone is presenting his words. That voice will be heard again in 7:27 and at the end of the book (12:8-14), and it is the frame through which the whole book must be read.

verseByVerse.quote: What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun?

Here is the question that drives the book. Gain is what is left over when everything is added up, the profit that remains. After a lifetime of work, what do you have that lasts?

Two phrases in the verse will return again and again. Toil is not just a job; it is the whole effort of a life, with the sweat and weariness that God spoke of when he said to Adam, cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life (Gen 3:17). And under the sun, which appears twenty-eight times in the ESV of this book, is the Preacher's vantage point. He looks at life on the level of the world as anyone can see it: the sun rising, people working, people dying. What can be proved from there alone?

His answer, for now, is nothing. And he is right. If this life is all there is, there is no final profit in it. Jesus asked the same question in sharper form: For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? (Matt 16:26).

But the question is not left hanging forever. After Christ rose from the dead, Paul could write the one sentence that answers verse 3: Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain (1 Cor 15:58). Under the sun, toil evaporates. In the Lord, it does not. Ecclesiastes does not yet say that. It makes us need it.

verseByVerse.quote: A generation goes, and a generation comes, but the earth remains forever. The sun rises, and the sun goes down, and hastens to the place where it rises. The wind blows to the south and goes around to the north; around and around goes the wind, and on its circuits the wind returns. All streams run to the sea, but the sea is not full; to the place where the streams flow, there they flow again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A generation goes, and a generation comes, but the earth remains forever.

The Preacher now looks at the world, and the first thing he sees is people coming and going. Stand in a cemetery and read the dates: generation after generation walked these same streets, and the streets outlasted all of them. The irony is sharp. Man was made to rule the earth, and the earth outlives man.

The sun rises, and the sun goes down, and hastens to the place where it rises.

Psalm 19 sees the sun as a strong man who runs its course with joy (Ps 19:5). The Preacher sees the same sun and feels its weariness. The ESV notes that hastens may be rendered "returns panting": the sun struggles back round to where it started, only to do it all again tomorrow.

The wind blows to the south and goes around to the north; around and around goes the wind, and on its circuits the wind returns. All streams run to the sea, but the sea is not full; to the place where the streams flow, there they flow again.

Wind circles; water flows and flows and never fills the sea. Every part of creation is busy, and none of it arrives anywhere. This is the world as a treadmill. And the Preacher means us to see ourselves in it, because human toil has the same shape: you get up, work, sleep, get up and do it again, and the inbox fills back up.

Is this how God sees the world? Not finally. The same sun knows its time for setting because God appointed it (Ps 104:19). Paul says creation really was subjected to futility after the fall, but because of him who subjected it, in hope (Rom 8:20). The treadmill is real. It is also not the last word.

verseByVerse.quote: All things are full of weariness; a man cannot utter it; the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All things are full of weariness; a man cannot utter it; the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.

Now the weariness moves inside. The world is tiring, and it is also more tiring than words can say: a man cannot utter it. And the human appetite that should rest in what it takes in never does. The eye is not satisfied with seeing. Scroll through another hundred images and the eye wants the next one. Hear the new song and the ear is already waiting for another.

Proverbs says the same with a darker comparison: Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and never satisfied are the eyes of man (Prov 27:20). The grave is never full, and neither is the human heart. We were made with an appetite that nothing under the sun can fill.

That is not a defect in us; it is a clue. Jesus stood by a well and said, Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again, but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again (John 4:13-14). Here is a test for any thing you are hoping will finally satisfy you: has anything like it ever satisfied you for long?

verseByVerse.quote: What has been is what will be, and what has been done is what will be done, and there is nothing new under the sun. Is there a thing of which it is said, "See, this is new"? It has been already in the ages before us. There is no remembrance of former things, nor will there be any remembrance of later things yet to be among those who come after.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What has been is what will be, and what has been done is what will be done, and there is nothing new under the sun.

Technology changes. The human story does not. The same pride, the same lust, the same greed and the same grief are acted out in every generation with new props. Every age thinks it has discovered something that will finally change what people are, and every age dies.

Is there a thing of which it is said, "See, this is new"? It has been already in the ages before us.

The Preacher anticipates the objection. Someone points to the latest thing and says, See, this is new. Look closer, he says, and you will find it has been done before. The claim to be new is itself very old.

Only one voice in Scripture can truly say it. At the end of the Bible, the one seated on the throne says, Behold, I am making all things new (Rev 21:5). Newness does not come up from under the sun. It comes down. And it has already begun: if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come (2 Cor 5:17).

There is no remembrance of former things, nor will there be any remembrance of later things yet to be among those who come after.

The ESV notes that former things and later things may be rendered "former people" and "later people". Either way the sting is the same. You will be forgotten. Try naming your great-great-grandparents. Most people cannot, and they lived only a century ago. Under the sun, even the memory of a life is breath. The comfort of the believer is that he is not remembered by history, but by God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–18 — The King Who Searched and Found Sorrow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Preacher was king over Israel in Jerusalem, and he set his heart to search out by wisdom everything done under heaven (vv. 12-13). What he found was vanity and a striving after wind; the crooked cannot be straightened (vv. 14-15). He had great wisdom and studied madness and folly as well (vv. 16-17), and learned that in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom can see how broken the world is, but it cannot mend it. Only the one who made the world can make the crooked straight.

verseByVerse.quote: I the Preacher have been king over Israel in Jerusalem. And I applied my heart to seek and to search out by wisdom all that is done under heaven. It is an unhappy business that God has given to the children of man to be busy with.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I the Preacher have been king over Israel in Jerusalem.

Having shown us the world, the Preacher now tells us his own story. He writes as a man who had every advantage for the search he is about to describe: a throne, a capital city, wealth, time and the best minds of the kingdom at his call.

And I applied my heart to seek and to search out by wisdom all that is done under heaven.

The ESV's note explains that the Hebrew term for heart denotes the centre of a person's inner life, including mind, will and emotions. This was not an idle hobby. He gave himself, all of himself, to understanding life. He did it by wisdom, the best tool human beings have.

It is an unhappy business that God has given to the children of man to be busy with.

And here God is named for the first time in the book. It is God who has given this business, and the Preacher calls it unhappy. That is honest. The drive to understand our lives is itself a burden, because we ask questions we cannot answer. Notice what he does not do. He does not say there is no God. He says God has laid this weight on us, and he feels it. Faith in Ecclesiastes is not the absence of hard questions. It is holding on to God while asking them.

verseByVerse.quote: I have seen everything that is done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and a striving after wind. What is crooked cannot be made straight, and what is lacking cannot be counted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have seen everything that is done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and a striving after wind.

The result of the king's search is the same verdict as verse 2, with a new picture added. A striving after wind, the ESV notes, may be rendered "a feeding on wind", and the note points to Hosea, where Ephraim feeds on the wind and pursues the east wind all day long (Hos 12:1). Try to catch the wind, and you close your hand on air. Try to live on it, and you starve.

What is crooked cannot be made straight, and what is lacking cannot be counted.

Here is what the wisest man in Israel found out: wisdom can diagnose, but it cannot cure. It can see that a marriage is bent, a nation corrupt, a heart twisted. It cannot straighten them. It can see what is missing in a life, and it cannot add it back. You cannot count what is not there.

The Preacher will say it again, and name who bent it: Consider the work of God: who can make straight what he has made crooked? (7:13). The answer is that no man can, but God can. When John the Baptist prepared the way for Christ, the promise was that the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places shall become level ways (Luke 3:5). What wisdom cannot mend, the Lord who came can.

Think of the thing in your own life you have tried longest to straighten. Verse 15 is not a counsel of despair. It is permission to stop pretending you can fix it alone.

verseByVerse.quote: I said in my heart, "I have acquired great wisdom, surpassing all who were over Jerusalem before me, and my heart has had great experience of wisdom and knowledge." And I applied my heart to know wisdom and to know madness and folly. I perceived that this also is but a striving after wind. For in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I said in my heart, "I have acquired great wisdom, surpassing all who were over Jerusalem before me, and my heart has had great experience of wisdom and knowledge."

He is not boasting idly. Scripture says of Solomon that he was wiser than all other men (1 Kgs 4:31). The Preacher is laying out his credentials so that his conclusion cannot be dismissed. This is not a man who never studied. It is a man who studied more than anyone.

And I applied my heart to know wisdom and to know madness and folly. I perceived that this also is but a striving after wind.

He studied both sides. Wisdom and folly, sense and madness, he examined them all, the way someone might read every philosophy on the shelf, looking for the key. And even the study of wisdom itself turned out to be chasing wind.

For in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow.

The more you know, the more it hurts. The child is happy in the car because he does not know about the mortgage. The doctor knows what the shadow on the scan means. The more clearly a person sees the world, the more clearly he sees the injustice, the waste and the death in it. Knowledge without redemption is a sharper pain.

So Paul says that the world did not know God through wisdom, and it pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe (1 Cor 1:21). Human wisdom climbs to the top of the ladder and finds only sorrow there. God comes down.

And when he came, he took the sorrow on himself. The one who knew more than anyone, who knew every heart and every grief, was a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief (Isa 53:3). He increased in knowledge, and carried the sorrow of it, so that those who come to him might find in him what the Preacher could not find under the sun: Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1 Cor 1:30).

1.overview:
The Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem, opens with his verdict: All is vanity (vv. 1-2). The word means mist or breath, something real but impossible to hold. Then comes the question the whole book is asking: What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun? (v. 3).

The world is an endless round. Generations come and go, the sun rises and sets, the wind circles and the streams run to a sea that is never full (vv. 4-7). The eye and ear are never satisfied, nothing is new, and nobody is remembered (vv. 8-11).

The Preacher then tells his own story. As king he set his heart to search out everything under heaven by wisdom (vv. 12-13). He found that all is a striving after wind, that the crooked cannot be made straight, and that increasing knowledge only increases sorrow (vv. 14-18).
1.theology:
Life viewed only under the sun yields no lasting gain (v. 3). Creation has been subjected to futility since the fall, but in hope (Rom 8:20), and the Preacher never says that there is no God; he says that God has given this burden (v. 13).

Human wisdom can diagnose what is crooked but cannot straighten it (v. 15; 7:13). God does what wisdom cannot: the crooked is made straight in the coming of Christ (Luke 3:5), who makes all things new (Rev 21:5; 2 Cor 5:17), and in whom labour is not in vain (1 Cor 15:58).

The restless eye (v. 8) shows that people are made for more than the world can give (John 4:13-14). The wisest son of David asks the question; something greater than Solomon is its answer (Matt 12:42; 1 Cor 1:30).
1.examples:
Your breath on a cold morning: visible, real, and gone when you try to grasp it.

Reading the dates in a cemetery.

The inbox that fills back up.

Scrolling for the next image.

Trying to name your great-great-grandparents.

The child happy in the car, and the parent who knows about the mortgage.

2.title: The King's Experiment: Pleasure, Greatness and the Hand of God

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Experiment with Pleasure and Greatness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Preacher tests his heart with pleasure and finds it vanity (vv. 1-2). He tries wine while keeping his wisdom, and then builds on a royal scale: houses, vineyards, gardens, pools, slaves, herds, silver and gold, singers (vv. 3-8). He surpasses all before him and denies his eyes nothing (vv. 9-10). Then he looks at it all: behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind, and there was nothing to be gained under the sun (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The man who had everything the world can offer is the best witness that the world cannot satisfy.

verseByVerse.quote: I said in my heart, "Come now, I will test you with pleasure; enjoy yourself." But behold, this also was vanity. I said of laughter, "It is mad," and of pleasure, "What use is it?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I said in my heart, "Come now, I will test you with pleasure; enjoy yourself." But behold, this also was vanity.

Chapter 1 ended with the discovery that more knowledge brings more sorrow. So the Preacher tries the obvious alternative. If thinking hurts, stop thinking and start enjoying. He speaks to his own heart like a friend with a plan: Come now, let us try pleasure.

Notice that he calls it a test. This is a deliberate experiment, and Ecclesiastes records the result before it describes the method: this also was vanity. Breath again. The ESV's note carries the same word, hebel, through this whole chapter.

I said of laughter, "It is mad," and of pleasure, "What use is it?"

Laughter is good; the Preacher is not a killjoy, as the end of this chapter will prove. But laughter pursued as the meaning of life is mad. Everyone knows the party where the laughter gets louder as the evening goes on and emptier with every glass. Pleasure asks to be taken as an answer, and when it is questioned, What use is it?, it has nothing to say.

Our culture has run this experiment on a scale no ancient king could imagine, and the result has not changed. Paul's description of the last days includes people who are lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God (2 Tim 3:4). Pleasure is a wonderful gift and a cruel god.

verseByVerse.quote: I searched with my heart how to cheer my body with wine—my heart still guiding me with wisdom—and how to lay hold on folly, till I might see what was good for the children of man to do under heaven during the few days of their life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I searched with my heart how to cheer my body with wine—my heart still guiding me with wisdom—and how to lay hold on folly, till I might see what was good for the children of man to do under heaven during the few days of their life.

This is not a man falling into drunkenness. It is a scientist conducting an experiment on himself. He drinks, but with my heart still guiding me with wisdom. He tries folly, but deliberately, to see what it is like. He wants to know one thing: what is actually good for the children of man to do in the few days of their life?

That last phrase sets the stakes. Life is short. If there is a way to spend it well, it matters enormously to find it. Moses prayed, So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom (Ps 90:12). The Preacher is numbering his days and asking how to fill them.

There is a warning here too. Many people have told themselves they could taste folly while keeping their head. The Preacher may have managed it. Most do not. The prodigal son also went looking for life in a far country and squandered his property in reckless living (Luke 15:13).

verseByVerse.quote: I made great works. I built houses and planted vineyards for myself. I made myself gardens and parks, and planted in them all kinds of fruit trees. I made myself pools from which to water the forest of growing trees. I bought male and female slaves, and had slaves who were born in my house. I had also great possessions of herds and flocks, more than any who had been before me in Jerusalem. I also gathered for myself silver and gold and the treasure of kings and provinces. I got singers, both men and women, and many concubines, the delight of the sons of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I made great works. I built houses and planted vineyards for myself. I made myself gardens and parks, and planted in them all kinds of fruit trees. I made myself pools from which to water the forest of growing trees.

Pleasure in the narrow sense was not enough, so the king moves on to achievement. Listen to the repeated words: I made, I built, for myself, I made myself. He builds a private paradise: gardens, parks, fruit trees of every kind, and pools to water a forest. It is as if he were trying to build Eden again with his own hands.

I bought male and female slaves, and had slaves who were born in my house. I had also great possessions of herds and flocks, more than any who had been before me in Jerusalem. I also gathered for myself silver and gold and the treasure of kings and provinces. I got singers, both men and women, and many concubines, the delight of the sons of man.

Then people, livestock, money, art and sex. Everything a man can own, he owned. The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew word behind many concubines is uncertain, but the phrase that follows is clear enough: the delight of the sons of man. He had every delight.

Scripture records that King Solomon excelled all the kings of the earth in riches and in wisdom (1 Kgs 10:23). This list is what the modern dream looks like when it is fully achieved: the house, the land, the portfolio, the staff, the entertainment, the lovers. Most people never get it, and imagine that if they did, they would be satisfied. The Preacher got it.

verseByVerse.quote: So I became great and surpassed all who were before me in Jerusalem. Also my wisdom remained with me. And whatever my eyes desired I did not keep from them. I kept my heart from no pleasure, for my heart found pleasure in all my toil, and this was my reward for all my toil. Then I considered all that my hands had done and the toil I had expended in doing it, and behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind, and there was nothing to be gained under the sun.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I became great and surpassed all who were before me in Jerusalem. Also my wisdom remained with me.

He reached the top. And he kept his head while doing it. The experiment was not spoiled by a man who lost his judgment on the way up.

And whatever my eyes desired I did not keep from them. I kept my heart from no pleasure, for my heart found pleasure in all my toil, and this was my reward for all my toil.

He is honest: it was enjoyable. My heart found pleasure in all my toil. There was real satisfaction in the building and the owning. But notice the limit of it: this was my reward. The pleasure of the work was all the work paid. Once the enjoyment was spent, nothing was left over.

Then I considered all that my hands had done and the toil I had expended in doing it, and behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind, and there was nothing to be gained under the sun.

Then comes the moment every achiever eventually meets. He stops and looks at it all. Everything he dreamed of stands finished in front of him, and he feels nothing. All was vanity. The athlete stands on the podium and wonders why it is not enough. The executive reaches the corner office and lies awake.

Jesus told of a rich man who did exactly what the Preacher did, and said to his soul, relax, eat, drink, be merry. But God said to him, 'Fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?' (Luke 12:19-20). Moses saw the same truth from the other side, choosing the people of God rather than the fleeting pleasures of sin, for he was looking to the reward (Heb 11:25-26).

Ask it plainly of your own ambitions: if you had all of it, what would you have?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — Wise and Fool Die Alike
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He turns to weigh wisdom against folly (v. 12). Wisdom really is better, as there is more gain in light than in darkness (vv. 13-14), And yet I perceived that the same event happens to all of them. The wise man dies like the fool and is forgotten like him (vv. 15-16), so I hated life (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom is better than folly for living, but under the sun it cannot answer death.

verseByVerse.quote: So I turned to consider wisdom and madness and folly. For what can the man do who comes after the king? Only what has already been done. Then I saw that there is more gain in wisdom than in folly, as there is more gain in light than in darkness. The wise person has his eyes in his head, but the fool walks in darkness. And yet I perceived that the same event happens to all of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I turned to consider wisdom and madness and folly. For what can the man do who comes after the king? Only what has already been done.

Pleasure failed, so he goes back to weigh wisdom. And he makes a point about his own experiment: no one after him can run it on a bigger scale. What can the man do who comes after the king? If a king with unlimited resources found it empty, no one else need try.

Then I saw that there is more gain in wisdom than in folly, as there is more gain in light than in darkness. The wise person has his eyes in his head, but the fool walks in darkness.

The Preacher is not against wisdom. It really is better. A wise person sees where he is walking; the fool walks into walls. Every word of Proverbs stands. Wisdom brings real gain, the same word as 1:3, for living.

And yet I perceived that the same event happens to all of them.

Then the And yet. Wisdom helps you walk through life. It cannot stop the road from ending in the same place. The same event, which he will name in a moment, is death. The wise and the fool walk different roads to the same grave.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said in my heart, "What happens to the fool will happen to me also. Why then have I been so very wise?" And I said in my heart that this also is vanity. For of the wise as of the fool there is no enduring remembrance, seeing that in the days to come all will have been long forgotten. How the wise dies just like the fool! So I hated life, because what is done under the sun was grievous to me, for all is vanity and a striving after wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I said in my heart, "What happens to the fool will happen to me also. Why then have I been so very wise?" And I said in my heart that this also is vanity.

The question becomes personal. He has spent his life becoming wise. The fool across the street spent his life doing nothing. And both will be buried. Why then have I been so very wise? It is the question of the student who worked hard beside the one who never did, and then watched both fail the same exam.

For of the wise as of the fool there is no enduring remembrance, seeing that in the days to come all will have been long forgotten. How the wise dies just like the fool!

Not only death, but forgetting. The wise man may be remembered a little longer, but not for long. The cry How the wise dies just like the fool! is almost a lament. Psalm 49 says the same: For he sees that even the wise die; the fool and the stupid alike must perish and leave their wealth to others (Ps 49:10).

So I hated life, because what is done under the sun was grievous to me, for all is vanity and a striving after wind.

These are some of the most honest words in the Bible. I hated life. The Preacher does not pretend. Some readers of this commentary know what it is to lie awake and feel exactly this, and it matters that God put these words in his book. You are not the first believer to feel it, and the feeling is not the end of the story.

He hated life under the sun, life seen from that level alone. That is the qualifier to hold onto. Everything under the sun ends in death. But God has not left us under the sun alone: it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment (Heb 9:27), and Christ came to deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery (Heb 2:15).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He hates his toil, because he must leave it to someone who may be a fool (vv. 18-19). He gives his heart up to despair: a person who toiled with skill leaves everything to someone who never worked for it (vv. 20-21). For all his days are full of sorrow, and his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest (vv. 22-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything gathered for self is finally handed to someone else.

verseByVerse.quote: I hated all my toil in which I toil under the sun, seeing that I must leave it to the man who will come after me, and who knows whether he will be wise or a fool? Yet he will be master of all for which I toiled and used my wisdom under the sun. This also is vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I hated all my toil in which I toil under the sun, seeing that I must leave it to the man who will come after me, and who knows whether he will be wise or a fool? Yet he will be master of all for which I toiled and used my wisdom under the sun. This also is vanity.

Now he looks at the future of his achievements. Everything he built will be left to someone else, and he has no control over what that person is like. A man spends forty years building a business, and his heir sells it in three. A woman saves carefully all her life, and the estate is fought over by relatives she barely knew.

For a son of David these words are painful. Solomon's own son Rehoboam came to the throne and answered the people harshly, and forsaking the counsel that the old men had given him (1 Kgs 12:13), and the kingdom his father had built was torn in two. Who knows whether he will be wise or a fool? Solomon did not know. Nobody does.

Man heaps up wealth and does not know who will gather! (Ps 39:6). The only safe inheritance is one that cannot be squandered: lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal (Matt 6:20).

verseByVerse.quote: So I turned about and gave my heart up to despair over all the toil of my labors under the sun, because sometimes a person who has toiled with wisdom and knowledge and skill must leave everything to be enjoyed by someone who did not toil for it. This also is vanity and a great evil. What has a man from all the toil and striving of heart with which he toils beneath the sun? For all his days are full of sorrow, and his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest. This also is vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I turned about and gave my heart up to despair over all the toil of my labors under the sun, because sometimes a person who has toiled with wisdom and knowledge and skill must leave everything to be enjoyed by someone who did not toil for it. This also is vanity and a great evil.

The Preacher reaches the bottom: despair. He calls it not only vanity but a great evil. It feels wrong, and it is wrong, that skill and wisdom and years of labour should be handed to someone who did nothing. Under the sun, there is no justice in inheritance.

What has a man from all the toil and striving of heart with which he toils beneath the sun? For all his days are full of sorrow, and his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest. This also is vanity.

The question of 1:3 returns, and this time with the cost added. Work done for self alone consumes the worker. His days are sorrow, his work is vexation, and Even in the night his heart does not rest. Anyone who has lain awake at three in the morning running through the numbers knows this verse.

The psalmist names the cure: It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep (Ps 127:2). The sleepless night is not a sign that you care enough. It is often a sign that you are carrying what only God can carry.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–26 — Nothing Better: From the Hand of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: There is nothing better for a person than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God (v. 24), for apart from him who can eat or who can have enjoyment? (v. 25). God gives wisdom, knowledge and joy to the one who pleases him, and the sinner gathers for someone else (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: Joy cannot be seized from the world; it is received from the hand of God.

verseByVerse.quote: There is nothing better for a person than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God, for apart from him who can eat or who can have enjoyment?
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is nothing better for a person than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God,

And then, suddenly, light. After despair, the Preacher says something that sounds completely different. There is nothing better than to eat, drink and enjoy your work. This is the first of several such passages in the book (3:12-13, 22; 5:18-20; 8:15; 9:7-10), and they are the thread of hope running through it.

What has changed? One phrase: from the hand of God. The experiment of verses 1-11 tried to seize enjoyment from the world, and it evaporated. Here enjoyment is received from God as a gift, and it is good. The same bread and wine, the same work, taste different when they come from a Father's hand. The ESV notes that find enjoyment may be rendered "make his soul see good": God opens the soul's eyes to the good that is in front of it.

This is not the rich fool's eat, drink, be merry, which leaves God out. It is Paul's God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Tim 6:17), and whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God (1 Cor 10:31).

for apart from him who can eat or who can have enjoyment?

Without God, no one can truly enjoy anything. The rich man with every delight could not. The ESV notes that most Hebrew manuscripts read "apart from me", while some manuscripts and ancient translations read apart from him. On the second reading, which the ESV follows, the verse makes the point directly: enjoyment is God's to give. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above (Jas 1:17). Tonight's supper can be received that way.

verseByVerse.quote: For to the one who pleases him God has given wisdom and knowledge and joy, but to the sinner he has given the business of gathering and collecting, only to give to one who pleases God. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For to the one who pleases him God has given wisdom and knowledge and joy, but to the sinner he has given the business of gathering and collecting, only to give to one who pleases God. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.

Two people, two gifts. To the one who pleases God, he gives wisdom and knowledge and joy: the very things the king could not get by his own effort. To the sinner, he gives busyness: gathering and collecting, only to hand it over in the end to someone else. Proverbs has the same pattern: the sinner's wealth is laid up for the righteous (Prov 13:22).

Who pleases God? Not the one who earns it, but the one who trusts him. The New Testament is clear that without faith it is impossible to please him, and the joy offered here is the joy of a person who has stopped trying to wring meaning out of the world and received it from God.

Then the chapter ends, surprisingly, with the refrain: This also is vanity and a striving after wind. Probably it refers to the sinner's gathering. But it also keeps the reader honest. Even God's good gifts under the sun are breath: the meal ends, the work is finished, the joy passes. They are good, and they are not God. So the psalmist's words are the right ending to this chapter: Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you (Ps 73:25).
