And he is father of a son, but he has nothing in his hand.<sup>15</sup>As he came from his mother's womb he shall go again, naked as he came, and shall take nothing for his toil that he may carry away in his hand.<sup>16</sup>This also is a grievous evil: just as he came, so shall he go, and what gain is there to him who toils for the wind?<sup>17</sup>Moreover, all his days he eats in darkness in much vexation and sickness and anger.<sup>18</sup>Behold, what I have seen to be good and fitting is to eat and drink and find enjoyment in all the toil with which one toils under the sun the few days of his life that God has given him, for this is his lot.<sup>19</sup>Everyone also to whom God has given wealth and possessions and power to enjoy them, and to accept his lot and rejoice in his toil—this is the gift of God.<sup>20</sup>For he will not much remember the days of his life because God keeps him occupied with joy in his heart.
5.overview:
The Preacher turns to worship. Guard your steps when you go to the house of God; listening is better than the sacrifice of fools (v. 1). Because God is in heaven and you are on earth, words before him should be few (vv. 2-3). A vow to God must be paid, and it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay (vv. 4-6). Many words are vanity, but God is the one you must fear (v. 7).

Oppression by officials should not surprise, for officials watch officials (vv. 8-9). He who loves money will not be satisfied with money; more goods bring more eaters, and the rich man cannot sleep (vv. 10-12). Hoarded riches are lost, and everyone leaves as naked as he came (vv. 13-17).

What is good and fitting is to eat, drink and enjoy one's toil in the days God gives. The power to enjoy wealth and accept one's lot is the gift of God, who keeps such a person occupied with joy (vv. 18-20).
5.theology:
Worship begins with listening and reverent fear, not many words (vv. 1-7; 1 Sam 15:22; Matt 6:7). God is in heaven, and in Christ believers may draw near with confidence and with reverence (Heb 4:16; 12:28-29). Promises to God are binding (vv. 4-6; Deut 23:21-23; Matt 5:37).

All earthly authority is accountable to a higher, and finally to God (vv. 8-9; Ps 82:1). The love of money cannot be satisfied and brings misery (vv. 10-17; 1 Tim 6:6-10); everyone leaves the world with nothing (v. 15; Job 1:21). Wealth, the power to enjoy it and contentment with one's lot are separate gifts of God (vv. 18-20; 1 Tim 6:17).
5.examples:
Coming to church to say your piece rather than to hear.

Promises made in hospital waiting rooms.

The lottery winner for whom enough keeps moving.

The labourer asleep and the rich man lying awake.

There are no pockets in a shroud.

A child too absorbed in play to watch the clock.

6.title: Wealth Without Enjoyment

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Wealth Without the Power to Enjoy It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A grievous evil: a man to whom God gives wealth, possessions, and honor, yet God does not give him power to enjoy them, and a stranger enjoys them (vv. 1-2). A man with a hundred children and many years, unsatisfied and unburied, is worse off than a stillborn child (vv. 3-5). Even two thousand years without good end in the one place (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Having everything is not the same as enjoying anything; enjoyment is a separate gift of God.

verseByVerse.quote: There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, and it lies heavy on mankind: a man to whom God gives wealth, possessions, and honor, so that he lacks nothing of all that he desires, yet God does not give him power to enjoy them, but a stranger enjoys them. This is vanity; it is a grievous evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, and it lies heavy on mankind:

Chapter 5 ended with the gift of joy. Chapter 6 shows its absence, and the Preacher says the evil lies heavy on mankind. This is not a rare case. It is common.

a man to whom God gives wealth, possessions, and honor, so that he lacks nothing of all that he desires, yet God does not give him power to enjoy them, but a stranger enjoys them. This is vanity; it is a grievous evil.

Here is the man who has everything. God has given him wealth, possessions, and honor. He lacks nothing. And God does not give him power to enjoy them. Put this beside 5:19, where the power to enjoy is the gift of God. Wealth and enjoyment are two different gifts. God can give the first and withhold the second.

That is one of the most searching truths in the book. Many people are praying for the first gift and never think to ask for the second. They imagine that if they only had the house, the job, the spouse, the money, they would be happy. But the capacity to be happy in them is not included in the purchase. It comes from God. And the man who has it all without that capacity watches a stranger enjoy what he worked for. Ask God for what you want if you must. Ask him first for a heart that can receive with joy what he has already given.

verseByVerse.quote: If a man fathers a hundred children and lives many years, so that the days of his years are many, but his soul is not satisfied with life's good things, and he also has no burial, I say that a stillborn child is better off than he. For it comes in vanity and goes in darkness, and in darkness its name is covered. Moreover, it has not seen the sun or known anything, yet it finds rest rather than he.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If a man fathers a hundred children and lives many years, so that the days of his years are many, but his soul is not satisfied with life's good things, and he also has no burial, I say that a stillborn child is better off than he.

In Israel, many children and long life were the highest blessings a man could have. Here a man has both, in exaggerated measure: a hundred children, many years. But his soul is not satisfied, and at the end he is not even buried with honour. Scripture treats an unburied body as disgrace; Jeremiah said of a faithless king, With the burial of a donkey he shall be buried (Jer 22:19). The man with everything ends with nothing, not even mourners.

And the Preacher's verdict is shocking: a stillborn child is better off than he.

For it comes in vanity and goes in darkness, and in darkness its name is covered. Moreover, it has not seen the sun or known anything, yet it finds rest rather than he.

The stillborn child never saw the light, never had a name spoken, never knew anything. Yet it finds rest. The rich man, who had everything, never did.

Parents who have lost a child before birth may find these verses hard to read, and they deserve a word. The Preacher is not saying the child's life did not matter. He is saying, from under the sun, that even the shortest life is not the worst fate. The worst fate is a long life with a restless soul. And the God who knows the name that was never spoken aloud has not lost that child.

verseByVerse.quote: Even though he should live a thousand years twice over, yet enjoy no good—do not all go to the one place?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even though he should live a thousand years twice over, yet enjoy no good—do not all go to the one place?

Double the longest life in Scripture, and more. Two thousand years. If a man enjoy no good, and the ESV notes that this may be rendered "see" no good, what has length added? Nothing, because all go to the one place (3:20).

Length of life is not the measure of it. A long life without joy is only a long walk to the same grave. A short life lived with God is full. Our culture spends fortunes trying to add years to life. The verse asks whether we have thought as hard about adding life to our years.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Who Knows What Is Good for Man?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All the toil of man is for his mouth, yet his appetite is not satisfied (v. 7). The wise and the poor have no final advantage (v. 8); what is in front of the eyes is better than wandering desire (v. 9). Man cannot dispute with one stronger than he, and more words only add vanity (vv. 10-11). For who knows what is good for man while he lives the few days of his vain life, which he passes like a shadow? (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: The book's first half ends with a question only God can answer.

verseByVerse.quote: All the toil of man is for his mouth, yet his appetite is not satisfied. For what advantage has the wise man over the fool? And what does the poor man have who knows how to conduct himself before the living? Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the appetite: this also is vanity and a striving after wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the toil of man is for his mouth, yet his appetite is not satisfied.

We work to eat, and we eat, and we are hungry again. The ESV notes that satisfied is in Hebrew "filled". The appetite is like a vessel with a hole in the bottom. And it is not only the stomach. The deeper appetite of the soul is never filled by what we work for. Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy? (Isa 55:2).

Jesus spoke to exactly this: Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you (John 6:27).

For what advantage has the wise man over the fool? And what does the poor man have who knows how to conduct himself before the living?

The wise man's appetite is as unfilled as the fool's. The poor man who has learned good manners and good sense still goes hungry. Under the sun, wisdom and decency do not fill the hole.

Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the appetite: this also is vanity and a striving after wind.

Here is practical wisdom, if not a final answer. Be content with what is in front of your eyes, rather than letting your desire wander after what you do not have. A bird in the hand. The meal on the table rather than the one in the advertisement. Yet even that contentment, on its own, is breath. It helps; it does not save.

verseByVerse.quote: Whatever has come to be has already been named, and it is known what man is, and that he is not able to dispute with one stronger than he. The more words, the more vanity, and what is the advantage to man?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever has come to be has already been named, and it is known what man is, and that he is not able to dispute with one stronger than he.

In Scripture, to name something is often to know it and to have authority over it. God determines the number of the stars; he gives to all of them their names (Ps 147:4). Everything that exists has already been named, known and defined by God. And it is known what man is: a creature, made from the dust, and not God.

So man cannot argue with one stronger than he. He cannot take God to court and win. Isaiah said, Woe to him who strives with him who formed him (Isa 45:9), and Paul, But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? (Rom 9:20).

The more words, the more vanity, and what is the advantage to man?

Arguments with God multiply words, and words multiply breath. This echoes 5:2-3. When we cannot understand God, the answer is not more talk, but trust. Job came to the same place: after all his speeches, he laid his hand on his mouth.

verseByVerse.quote: For who knows what is good for man while he lives the few days of his vain life, which he passes like a shadow? For who can tell man what will be after him under the sun?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For who knows what is good for man while he lives the few days of his vain life, which he passes like a shadow? For who can tell man what will be after him under the sun?

The first half of Ecclesiastes ends with two questions, and they are the right questions. What is good for us, in our short, breath-like life? The ESV's note marks vain as hebel again: a breath of a life. And what will happen after we are gone?

Life passes like a shadow. David prayed, Our days on the earth are like a shadow, and there is no abiding (1 Chr 29:15). Man is like a breath; his days are like a passing shadow (Ps 144:4).

From under the sun, no one can answer these questions. That is the whole point. Chapters 7-12 will offer wisdom for how to live, but the final answer to "who knows what is good for man?" must come from above. And it has. He has told you, O man, what is good (Mic 6:8). And it has come in a person, who said, I came that they may have life and have it abundantly (John 10:10). The shadow is not the end for those who belong to him, because he is the light.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, and it lies heavy on mankind:<sup>2</sup>a man to whom God gives wealth, possessions, and honor, so that he lacks nothing of all that he desires, yet God does not give him power to enjoy them, but a stranger enjoys them. This is vanity; it is a grievous evil.<sup>3</sup>If a man fathers a hundred children and lives many years, so that the days of his years are many, but his soul is not satisfied with life's good things, and he also has no burial, I say that a stillborn child is better off than he.<sup>4</sup>For it comes in vanity and goes in darkness, and in darkness its name is covered.<sup>5</sup>Moreover, it has not seen the sun or known anything, yet it finds rest rather than he.<sup>6</sup>Even though he should live a thousand years twice over, yet enjoy no good—do not all go to the one place?<sup>7</sup>All the toil of man is for his mouth, yet his appetite is not satisfied.<sup>8</sup>For what advantage has the wise man over the fool? And what does the poor man have who knows how to conduct himself before the living?<sup>9</sup>Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the appetite: this also is vanity and a striving after wind.<sup>10</sup>Whatever has come to be has already been named, and it is known what man is, and that he is not able to dispute with one stronger than he.<sup>11</sup>The more words, the more vanity, and what is the advantage to man?<sup>12</sup>For who knows what is good for man while he lives the few days of his vain life, which he passes like a shadow? For who can tell man what will be after him under the sun?
6.overview:
The Preacher describes a heavy evil: a man to whom God gives wealth, possessions and honour, but not the power to enjoy them, so that a stranger enjoys them instead (vv. 1-2). A man with a hundred children and many years whose soul is unsatisfied, and who is not even buried, is worse off than a stillborn child, who at least finds rest (vv. 3-5). Two thousand years without good still end in the one place (v. 6).

Man toils for his mouth and his appetite is never filled; the wise and the poor fare no better (vv. 7-8). What the eyes see is better than wandering desire (v. 9). Man cannot dispute with the one who is stronger, and more words only add vanity (vv. 10-11). The chapter ends with two questions: who knows what is good for man in his shadow-like life, and who can tell what will come after him? (v. 12).
6.theology:
Wealth and the power to enjoy it are separate gifts of God; he may give one and withhold the other (v. 2; 5:19). Neither long life nor many children can satisfy the soul (vv. 3-6). Human appetite is never filled by what it works for (v. 7; Isa 55:2), but Christ gives food that endures to eternal life (John 6:27).

God has named and defined all things, and man cannot contend with his Maker (v. 10; Isa 45:9; Rom 9:20). Life is a shadow (v. 12; Ps 144:4), and what is good for man is revealed by God, not discovered under the sun (Mic 6:8; John 10:10).
6.examples:
Praying for the house and never for a heart to enjoy it.

A hundred children and no mourners.

Adding years to life, and forgetting to add life to the years.

An appetite like a vessel with a hole in the bottom.

The meal on the table rather than the one in the advertisement.

7.title: Better Things: Mourning, Patience and the Upright Made Crooked

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A good name is better than precious ointment, and the day of death than the day of birth (v. 1). The house of mourning teaches more than the house of feasting (vv. 2-4), and a wise rebuke more than a fool's song (vv. 5-7). Patience is better than pride and anger, and nostalgia is not wisdom (vv. 8-10). Wisdom protects like money (vv. 11-12). Consider the work of God: In the day of prosperity be joyful, and in the day of adversity consider, for God made both (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: The things that humble and sober us are often better for the soul than the things that please us.

verseByVerse.quote: A good name is better than precious ointment, and the day of death than the day of birth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A good name is better than precious ointment, and the day of death than the day of birth.

The first half of the book ended by asking, who knows what is good for man? (6:12). Chapter 7 begins to answer with a string of "better" sayings, and the first ones are startling.

Perfume is lovely, and it fades. A good name lasts. A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches (Prov 22:1). Then the shock: the day of death than the day of birth. At a birth, everything is possible and nothing is settled. At a death, the life is complete, and its name is known. For a person who has lived well, the funeral says more than the birth announcement ever could.

For the believer there is more still. The day of death is the day of going home. Paul could say, For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain, and My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better (Phil 1:21, 23). The Preacher could see only that the day of death finishes a life. The gospel shows that for those in Christ it begins a better one.

verseByVerse.quote: It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting, for this is the end of all mankind, and the living will lay it to heart. Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad. The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting, for this is the end of all mankind, and the living will lay it to heart.

Which invitation would you rather accept this weekend, the party or the funeral? Almost everyone chooses the party. The Preacher says the funeral is better for you. At the party you forget that you will die. At the funeral you remember, and the living will lay it to heart.

That is not morbid. It is wisdom. So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom (Ps 90:12). A person who has stood at a graveside and let it sink in makes different decisions on Monday.

Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad.

A paradox: sadness makes the heart glad. Not all sadness. But the sorrow that faces reality honestly does a deep work that laughter cannot. Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret (2 Cor 7:10). And Jesus said, Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted (Matt 5:4). The gladness on the other side of mourning is deeper than the gladness that avoids it.

The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth.

Where does your heart go when it is free to go anywhere? The fool's heart runs to entertainment, always, to avoid thinking. The wise heart is willing to sit with grief, its own and others'. Our culture has built a house of mirth that never closes, a screen in every pocket. Ask what it is helping you not to feel.

verseByVerse.quote: It is better for a man to hear the rebuke of the wise than to hear the song of fools. For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fools; this also is vanity. Surely oppression drives the wise into madness, and a bribe corrupts the heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is better for a man to hear the rebuke of the wise than to hear the song of fools.

A rebuke hurts, and a song is pleasant. But the wise friend who tells you the truth is doing you more good than a room full of people telling you what you want to hear. Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy (Prov 27:6). David prayed for such wounds: let him rebuke me—it is oil for my head (Ps 141:5). Who in your life is allowed to tell you that you are wrong?

For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fools; this also is vanity.

Dry thorns make a quick, loud blaze, and they are gone before the pot boils. So is the fool's laughter: loud, bright, and useless. Breath, as the ESV's note marks it.

Surely oppression drives the wise into madness, and a bribe corrupts the heart.

A warning to the wise. Even a wise man is not immune. Long pressure can drive him to act like a fool, and a bribe can bend his heart. For a bribe blinds the clear-sighted (Exod 23:8). Wisdom must be guarded, not assumed.

verseByVerse.quote: Better is the end of a thing than its beginning, and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit. Be not quick in your spirit to become angry, for anger lodges in the heart of fools. Say not, "Why were the former days better than these?" For it is not from wisdom that you ask this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Better is the end of a thing than its beginning, and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit.

Beginnings are exciting; endings show what a thing was. Anyone can start a marriage, a project, a Christian life. The end tells the truth. And what gets a person to a good end is patience, not pride. The proud want the result now and quit when it does not come. The patient keep going.

Be not quick in your spirit to become angry, for anger lodges in the heart of fools.

The ESV notes that in the heart is in Hebrew "in the bosom". Anger that is nursed and held close settles in and makes a home. Anger may flash in a wise person; it lodges in a fool. Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger (Eph 4:26), for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God (Jas 1:20).

Say not, "Why were the former days better than these?" For it is not from wisdom that you ask this.

Nostalgia feels wise, and it is not. The good old days were never as good as memory makes them. Israel in the wilderness remembered the fish we ate in Egypt that cost nothing (Num 11:5), and forgot the whips. The question is a way of refusing the present God has given. Paul's way is better: forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead (Phil 3:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Wisdom is good with an inheritance, an advantage to those who see the sun. For the protection of wisdom is like the protection of money, and the advantage of knowledge is that wisdom preserves the life of him who has it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom is good with an inheritance, an advantage to those who see the sun.

Wisdom and wealth together are a good combination. An inheritance without wisdom is soon wasted. With wisdom, it becomes a blessing to those still living, those who see the sun.

For the protection of wisdom is like the protection of money, and the advantage of knowledge is that wisdom preserves the life of him who has it.

Money gives a kind of shelter: against hunger, against emergencies. Wisdom does too. But wisdom has an advantage money lacks: it preserves the life of its owner. Money can be stolen, spent or lost in a bad venture (5:14). Wisdom keeps a person from walking into the disasters that money cannot repair.

verseByVerse.quote: Consider the work of God: who can make straight what he has made crooked? In the day of prosperity be joyful, and in the day of adversity consider: God has made the one as well as the other, so that man may not find out anything that will be after him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider the work of God: who can make straight what he has made crooked?

In 1:15 the Preacher said, What is crooked cannot be made straight. Here he says who bent it: God. Some things in your life God has made crooked: the illness, the disability, the child who was never born, the marriage that never came. You cannot straighten them, and you are not asked to. You are asked to consider the work of God, to look at them as his work and not as random chaos.

That is hard. It is also a comfort, because what God has bent, God can straighten, and one day will. The uneven ground shall become level, and the rough places a plain (Isa 40:4).

In the day of prosperity be joyful, and in the day of adversity consider: God has made the one as well as the other, so that man may not find out anything that will be after him.

Two kinds of days, and two responses. On a good day, rejoice; do not spoil it with worry about tomorrow. On a bad day, consider: think, reflect, remember who made this day. Both kinds come from the same hand. Job said, Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil? (Job 2:10). Is it not from the mouth of the Most High that good and bad come? (Lam 3:38).

And God mixes them so that man may not find out anything that will be after him. We cannot predict our lives, so we cannot trust in our predictions. We are left to trust God, who for those who love God makes all things work together for good (Rom 8:28).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–22 — The Fear of God Between Two Ditches
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The righteous sometimes perish and the wicked live long (v. 15). Be not overly righteous, Be not overly wicked, for the one who fears God shall come out from both of them (vv. 16-18). Wisdom strengthens, yet there is not a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins (vv. 19-20), so do not take to heart every word said against you (vv. 21-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The fear of God keeps a person from both self-righteousness and licence, and the knowledge of his own sin keeps him gentle.

verseByVerse.quote: In my vain life I have seen everything. There is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness, and there is a wicked man who prolongs his life in his evildoing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In my vain life I have seen everything. There is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness, and there is a wicked man who prolongs his life in his evildoing.

The Preacher faces what Proverbs, taken as a set of guarantees, cannot explain. A righteous man dies young, in his righteousness: not despite it, but while he is living it. A wicked man lives to ninety. The ESV's note marks vain as hebel: a breath of a life, and in it he has seen this.

Scripture does not hide it. The righteous man perishes, and no one lays it to heart (Isa 57:1). Jesus was asked about people who died in a disaster and said, do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others? (Luke 13:4). Suffering in this life is not a precise measure of sin. That is why this life cannot be the whole of justice.

verseByVerse.quote: Be not overly righteous, and do not make yourself too wise. Why should you destroy yourself? Be not overly wicked, neither be a fool. Why should you die before your time? It is good that you should take hold of this, and from that withhold not your hand, for the one who fears God shall come out from both of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be not overly righteous, and do not make yourself too wise. Why should you destroy yourself?

This verse is often misread as "don't be too religious". It cannot mean that; Scripture never warns against too much real holiness. The warning is against a self-made righteousness, a performance of goodness that tries to force God's hand and guarantee a good life. Seeing in verse 15 that the righteous sometimes perish, a person might try harder, stricter, more rules, more display, as if he could buy immunity. The Pharisee in the temple prayed, God, I thank you that I am not like other men (Luke 18:11). That road destroys a person: it breeds pride, exhaustion and harshness, and it never reaches God.

Be not overly wicked, neither be a fool. Why should you die before your time?

The opposite ditch. Having seen the wicked live long, a person might decide that goodness does not pay and throw himself into evil. That road also kills. Folly brings its own early grave.

It is good that you should take hold of this, and from that withhold not your hand, for the one who fears God shall come out from both of them.

The way between the ditches is not moderation, a little goodness and a little sin. It is the one who fears God. The fear of God frees a person from both performance and rebellion. He does not try to earn God's favour, and he does not despise it. He trusts God, obeys God, and leaves the outcome to God. That is the only road that comes out safely from both of them.

verseByVerse.quote: Wisdom gives strength to the wise man more than ten rulers who are in a city. Surely there is not a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom gives strength to the wise man more than ten rulers who are in a city.

A city with ten rulers has a great deal of power. The wise man, alone, has more. Wisdom is a stronger defence than a council of the powerful.

Surely there is not a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins.

And yet even the wise man sins. This verse is one of the clearest Old Testament statements of the universal sinfulness that the New Testament teaches. Solomon prayed at the temple dedication, for there is no one who does not sin (1 Kgs 8:46). Paul gathered the Old Testament's witness: None is righteous, no, not one (Rom 3:10). If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves (1 John 1:8).

It is also why verse 16 matters. No one can be righteous enough to guarantee anything. The only hope for a person who knows verse 20 is true is mercy, and mercy is offered: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not take to heart all the things that people say, lest you hear your servant cursing you. Your heart knows that many times you yourself have cursed others.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not take to heart all the things that people say, lest you hear your servant cursing you. Your heart knows that many times you yourself have cursed others.

A practical application of verse 20. People will say things about you: at work, in the family, online. Do not take it all to heart. If you go listening for every word, you will hear something cruel, even from someone who works for you.

And before you get indignant, remember your own mouth. Your heart knows how often you have spoken badly of others. Knowing your own sin makes you slower to be crushed by other people's words, and slower to condemn them. Judge not, that you be not judged (Matt 7:1). Grace received makes a thick skin and a soft heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–29 — Searching for Wisdom, Finding Sin
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Preacher tried to be wise, but wisdom was far off, and deep, very deep (vv. 23-24). Searching out folly, he found the seductress more bitter than death (vv. 25-26). Adding one thing to another, he found few upright (vv. 27-28). See, this alone I found, that God made man upright, but they have sought out many schemes (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology: The deepest thing the search uncovers is the fall: God made us upright, and we made ourselves crooked.

verseByVerse.quote: All this I have tested by wisdom. I said, "I will be wise," but it was far from me. That which has been is far off, and deep, very deep; who can find it out?
verseByVerse.commentary:
All this I have tested by wisdom. I said, "I will be wise," but it was far from me.

A confession from the wisest man in Jerusalem. He set out to be wise, and wisdom was far from me. The more he learned, the further off the full answer seemed.

That which has been is far off, and deep, very deep; who can find it out?

Reality itself is deep, very deep. Job asked, But where shall wisdom be found? and answered, it is not found in the land of the living (Job 28:12-13). Paul, at the end of his greatest argument, could only worship: Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments (Rom 11:33). The right response to a depth you cannot plumb is not despair, but humility.

verseByVerse.quote: I turned my heart to know and to search out and to seek wisdom and the scheme of things, and to know the wickedness of folly and the foolishness that is madness. And I find something more bitter than death: the woman whose heart is snares and nets, and whose hands are fetters. He who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is taken by her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I turned my heart to know and to search out and to seek wisdom and the scheme of things, and to know the wickedness of folly and the foolishness that is madness.

Once more he gives himself entirely to the search: to understand the scheme of things, how it all adds up, and also the nature of folly and wickedness.

And I find something more bitter than death: the woman whose heart is snares and nets, and whose hands are fetters. He who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is taken by her.

The first thing he finds is a trap. This is the seductress Proverbs warns against: For the lips of a forbidden woman drip honey, but in the end she is bitter as wormwood (Prov 5:3-4); Her house is the way to Sheol (Prov 7:27). Sexual sin promises sweetness and delivers bondage: snares and nets, fetters. Many men have found it more bitter than death, because it destroyed the marriage, the family and the name that death would have left intact.

And the escape is not cleverness. It is God: He who pleases God escapes her. The one who walks with God is kept.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, this is what I found, says the Preacher, while adding one thing to another to find the scheme of things— which my soul has sought repeatedly, but I have not found. One man among a thousand I found, but a woman among all these I have not found. See, this alone I found, that God made man upright, but they have sought out many schemes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, this is what I found, says the Preacher, while adding one thing to another to find the scheme of things— which my soul has sought repeatedly, but I have not found. One man among a thousand I found, but a woman among all these I have not found.

The frame narrator speaks again, says the Preacher, as in 1:2 and 12:8. And the Preacher reports what his search produced: almost nothing. He was looking for the truly upright person, and found One man among a thousand, and no woman.

This is a hard verse, and it must be read carefully. It is not the Bible's verdict on women. The same wisdom literature says He who finds a wife finds a good thing and obtains favor from the LORD (Prov 18:22), and celebrates the excellent wife as far more precious than jewels (Prov 31:10). The Preacher is reporting his own search in his own world, and his real point is how rare uprightness is at all: one in a thousand is almost none. The next verse makes clear that the problem he found is not one sex, but the whole race.

See, this alone I found, that God made man upright, but they have sought out many schemes.

Here is the one sure thing his search uncovered, and it is the doctrine of the fall in a sentence. God made man upright: humanity, male and female, created in God's image and called very good (Gen 1:27, 31). But they have sought out many schemes. The Preacher has been searching for the scheme of things; what human beings have produced is many schemes, endless inventions of their own for getting around God.

The world is not crooked because God made it badly. It is crooked because we bent it. Sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin (Rom 5:12). That is humbling, and it is also hopeful. What was made upright can be made upright again, and in Christ it is: you are all one in Christ Jesus (Gal 3:28), men and women alike, forgiven and renewed.
