7.overview:
The chapter begins to answer the question of 6:12 with "better" sayings. A good name is better than perfume, and the day of death than the day of birth (v. 1). The house of mourning teaches the heart more than the house of feasting (vv. 2-4); a wise rebuke is better than a fool's song (vv. 5-7); patience is better than pride and anger, and longing for former days is not wise (vv. 8-10). Wisdom protects like money and preserves life (vv. 11-12). God makes both the crooked and the straight, both prosperity and adversity (vv. 13-14).

The righteous sometimes perish and the wicked live long (v. 15). The Preacher warns against both self-made righteousness and wickedness, for the one who fears God escapes both (vv. 16-18). No one on earth does good and never sins, so do not take every criticism to heart (vv. 19-22).

Wisdom is far off and very deep (vv. 23-24). The Preacher finds the seductress more bitter than death, and finds uprightness almost nowhere (vv. 25-28). His one certain discovery: God made man upright, but they have sought out many schemes (v. 29).
7.theology:
Facing death and sorrow honestly produces wisdom (vv. 1-4; Ps 90:12; Matt 5:4); for believers, death is gain (Phil 1:21). God sovereignly ordains both prosperity and adversity (vv. 13-14; Lam 3:38) and works all things for good for those who love him (Rom 8:28).

The fear of God delivers from both self-righteousness and licence (vv. 16-18; Luke 18:11). All people sin (v. 20; 1 Kgs 8:46; Rom 3:10), and the only hope is God's forgiveness (1 John 1:9).

God created humanity upright, and humanity fell by its own schemes (v. 29; Gen 1:27, 31; Rom 5:12). The problem of sin belongs to men and women alike, and so does the remedy in Christ (Gal 3:28).
7.examples:
Choosing between the party and the funeral this weekend.

The friend who is allowed to tell you that you are wrong.

Thorns crackling under a pot.

Remembering the fish in Egypt and forgetting the whips.

The Pharisee's prayer, and the ditch on the other side of the road.

Listening for every word said about you.

8.title: The King's Word and the Delay of Justice

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Wise Man Before the King
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom makes a man's face shine (v. 1). Keep the king's command, do not rush from his presence or stand in an evil cause, for his word is supreme (vv. 2-4). The wise heart knows the proper time and the just way, though no one knows the future (vv. 5-7). No man has power to retain the spirit, or power over the day of death (v. 8), and the Preacher has seen man rule over man to his hurt (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Earthly rulers deserve wise submission, but every ruler stands powerless before death and before God.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is like the wise? And who knows the interpretation of a thing? A man's wisdom makes his face shine, and the hardness of his face is changed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who is like the wise? And who knows the interpretation of a thing? A man's wisdom makes his face shine, and the hardness of his face is changed.

Wisdom shows on the face. A person who understands what is going on, who knows the interpretation of a thing, has a brightness about him, and the hard, set expression of anxiety or pride is softened. We have all met people whose faces have been made gentle by years of walking wisely with God.

Moses came down from meeting God with his face shining. Paul says that something like it is happening to every believer: we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image (2 Cor 3:18). The wisdom that changes the face is finally the wisdom of knowing Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: I say: Keep the king's command, because of God's oath to him. Be not hasty to go from his presence. Do not take your stand in an evil cause, for he does whatever he pleases. For the word of the king is supreme, and who may say to him, "What are you doing?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I say: Keep the king's command, because of God's oath to him.

The ESV notes that I say is not in the Hebrew, and that the second half may be rendered "because of your oath to God". Either way, obedience to the king is tied to God. Either God has sworn to uphold the king, or the subject has sworn before God to be loyal. Civil obedience is a religious matter.

The New Testament says the same: Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God (Rom 13:1), and Fear God. Honor the emperor (1 Pet 2:17). A Christian is to be a good citizen, paying taxes, keeping laws, honouring rulers, not because rulers are always good, but because God ordains authority.

Be not hasty to go from his presence. Do not take your stand in an evil cause, for he does whatever he pleases. For the word of the king is supreme, and who may say to him, "What are you doing?"

A courtier's wisdom. Do not storm out of the king's presence in anger. Do not join a rebellion. The king has power, and resisting it rashly gets people killed.

But there is a limit, and Scripture marks it. When a king commands what God forbids, the answer is Peter's: We must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego honoured Nebuchadnezzar and refused his idol: But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods (Dan 3:18).

And notice the question who may say to him, "What are you doing?" It is true of an earthly king only for a while. It is true of God forever. Nebuchadnezzar himself learned to say of God, none can stay his hand or say to him, "What have you done?" (Dan 4:35).

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever keeps a command will know no evil thing, and the wise heart will know the proper time and the just way. For there is a time and a way for everything, although man's trouble lies heavy on him. For he does not know what is to be, for who can tell him how it will be?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever keeps a command will know no evil thing, and the wise heart will know the proper time and the just way.

Obedience keeps a person out of a great deal of trouble. And wisdom knows not only what to do, but when and how. The ESV notes that the just way may be rendered "judgment". Wisdom has timing. The right words at the wrong moment can be as foolish as the wrong words.

For there is a time and a way for everything, although man's trouble lies heavy on him. For he does not know what is to be, for who can tell him how it will be?

This echoes chapter 3: a time and a way for everything. But now with a weight added. The ESV notes that trouble may be rendered "evil". Knowing that there is a right time does not mean we know when it is. He does not know what is to be. That uncertainty presses on every decision.

James draws the Christian conclusion: you do not know what tomorrow will bring, so you ought to say, "If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that" (Jas 4:14-15). Uncertainty is meant to drive us to dependence.

verseByVerse.quote: No man has power to retain the spirit, or power over the day of death. There is no discharge from war, nor will wickedness deliver those who are given to it. All this I observed while applying my heart to all that is done under the sun, when man had power over man to his hurt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No man has power to retain the spirit, or power over the day of death. There is no discharge from war, nor will wickedness deliver those who are given to it.

The king has great power, but not this power. No one can hold on to his breath when it goes. No one can move the day of his death. You have appointed his limits that he cannot pass (Job 14:5). Death is a war with no discharge papers. And wickedness, which seemed to win so many battles, cannot win this one. The tyrant dies like the slave.

Truly no man can ransom another, or give to God the price of his life (Ps 49:7). Only one man ever had power over the day of his death. Jesus said of his life, I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again (John 10:18). He entered the war that has no discharge and won it, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death (Heb 2:14).

All this I observed while applying my heart to all that is done under the sun, when man had power over man to his hurt.

The Preacher sums up what he has seen: the power of man over man, and how often it is used to his hurt. Power in human hands tends toward harm. That is why the powerless need a King above all kings.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–15 — When the Sentence Is Delayed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wicked are buried with honour (v. 10). Because the sentence against an evil deed is not executed speedily, the heart of the children of man is fully set to do evil (v. 11). Yet it will be well with those who fear God and not with the wicked (vv. 12-13), though on earth the righteous and wicked sometimes receive each other's due (v. 14). And I commend joy (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: God's patience is not his indifference; judgment delayed is not judgment denied.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw the wicked buried. They used to go in and out of the holy place and were praised in the city where they had done such things. This also is vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I saw the wicked buried. They used to go in and out of the holy place and were praised in the city where they had done such things. This also is vanity.

A funeral with honours. The wicked man had been a regular at worship, in and out of the holy place, and at his burial the city praised him, the same city that had watched him do his evil. Every generation has seen the eulogy that bore no resemblance to the life.

The ESV notes that most Hebrew manuscripts read "forgotten" where some read praised. On that reading, the wicked were soon forgotten by the very city where they did their deeds. Either way, their end is breath. Jesus spoke of religious men who were like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people's bones (Matt 23:27). The city's praise does not settle anything. God's verdict does.

verseByVerse.quote: Because the sentence against an evil deed is not executed speedily, the heart of the children of man is fully set to do evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the sentence against an evil deed is not executed speedily, the heart of the children of man is fully set to do evil.

Here is one of the sharpest observations in the book about human nature. When punishment is slow, people conclude it is not coming, and their hearts become fully set to do evil. The child who is never corrected, the executive whose fraud goes unnoticed for years, the nation where crime goes unpunished: each learns to go further.

The same is true of how people treat God. Because judgment has not fallen, they assume it never will. But Scripture reads the delay the other way: The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance (2 Pet 3:9). The delay is mercy. To use it as permission is to be storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath (Rom 2:5). Is there a sin you continue in because nothing has happened yet?

verseByVerse.quote: Though a sinner does evil a hundred times and prolongs his life, yet I know that it will be well with those who fear God, because they fear before him. But it will not be well with the wicked, neither will he prolong his days like a shadow, because he does not fear before God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though a sinner does evil a hundred times and prolongs his life, yet I know that it will be well with those who fear God, because they fear before him.

Now the Preacher speaks as a believer. He has seen the sinner do evil a hundred times and live long. He does not deny it. Yet I know. Against all appearances, it will be well with those who fear God. This is not observation from under the sun. It is faith in what God has said. Tell the righteous that it shall be well with them (Isa 3:10).

But it will not be well with the wicked, neither will he prolong his days like a shadow, because he does not fear before God.

And the other side: it will not be well with the wicked. His long days are a shadow, which lengthens in the evening just before it vanishes. The dividing line in both verses is the same: fear before God. Not wealth, not length of life, not reputation. Fret not yourself because of evildoers, For they will soon fade like the grass (Ps 37:1-2).

verseByVerse.quote: There is a vanity that takes place on earth, that there are righteous people to whom it happens according to the deeds of the wicked, and there are wicked people to whom it happens according to the deeds of the righteous. I said that this also is vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is a vanity that takes place on earth, that there are righteous people to whom it happens according to the deeds of the wicked, and there are wicked people to whom it happens according to the deeds of the righteous. I said that this also is vanity.

The Preacher does not let faith become a slogan that ignores the facts. Right after it will be well with those who fear God, he admits again what we all see: the righteous sometimes get what the wicked deserve, and the wicked what the righteous deserve. The good man's business fails; the crook's thrives.

Both verses are true at once. Verses 12-13 speak of the end; verse 14 of the meantime. Malachi heard people say, It is vain to serve God, Evildoers not only prosper but they put God to the test and they escape, and God answered, Then once more you shall see the distinction between the righteous and the wicked (Mal 3:14-15, 18). Abraham said to the rich man, you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here (Luke 16:25). The meantime is not the end.

verseByVerse.quote: And I commend joy, for man has nothing better under the sun but to eat and drink and be joyful, for this will go with him in his toil through the days of his life that God has given him under the sun.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I commend joy, for man has nothing better under the sun but to eat and drink and be joyful, for this will go with him in his toil through the days of his life that God has given him under the sun.

After injustice, joy again. This is the fourth time the phrase nothing better appears in the book (2:24; 3:12, 22). It is not a shrug. It is a deliberate choice made in the face of everything he has just described. Precisely because the world is unjust and we cannot fix it or understand it, the Preacher commends joy: receive God's daily gifts with gladness, and let that joy go with him in his toil.

Joy in a broken world is not denial. It is trust. The same God who will set everything right has given this meal, this work, this day. When Nehemiah's people wept over their sins, he told them to eat, drink and send portions to those who had nothing, for the joy of the LORD is your strength (Neh 8:10). Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice (Phil 4:4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–17 — The Work of God No One Can Find Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Preacher gave his heart to know wisdom and watched the sleepless business of the earth (v. 16). Then I saw all the work of God, that man cannot find out the work that is done under the sun; Even though a wise man claims to know, he cannot find it out (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: The limit of human wisdom is not a failure of effort; it is the boundary between creature and Creator.

verseByVerse.quote: When I applied my heart to know wisdom, and to see the business that is done on earth, how neither day nor night do one's eyes see sleep, then I saw all the work of God, that man cannot find out the work that is done under the sun. However much man may toil in seeking, he will not find it out. Even though a wise man claims to know, he cannot find it out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I applied my heart to know wisdom, and to see the business that is done on earth, how neither day nor night do one's eyes see sleep,

The Preacher returns to his search, and to the sleepless busyness of the human race. Day and night people work, plan and worry.

then I saw all the work of God, that man cannot find out the work that is done under the sun. However much man may toil in seeking, he will not find it out. Even though a wise man claims to know, he cannot find it out.

Three times in one verse: cannot find out, will not find it out, cannot find it out. No amount of effort will uncover the full meaning of God's work. And the man who says he has, the wise man who claims to know, is mistaken.

This is not anti-intellectual. It is honest about the size of God. Behold, these are but the outskirts of his ways, and how small a whisper do we hear of him! (Job 26:14). The humble response is Moses': The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law (Deut 29:29). You do not need to understand God's whole work to trust him and obey what he has revealed.

8.text: <sup>1</sup>Who is like the wise? And who knows the interpretation of a thing? A man's wisdom makes his face shine, and the hardness of his face is changed.<sup>2</sup>I say: Keep the king's command, because of God's oath to him.<sup>3</sup>Be not hasty to go from his presence. Do not take your stand in an evil cause, for he does whatever he pleases.<sup>4</sup>For the word of the king is supreme, and who may say to him, "What are you doing?"<sup>5</sup>Whoever keeps a command will know no evil thing, and the wise heart will know the proper time and the just way.<sup>6</sup>For there is a time and a way for everything, although man's trouble lies heavy on him.<sup>7</sup>For he does not know what is to be, for who can tell him how it will be?<sup>8</sup>No man has power to retain the spirit, or power over the day of death. There is no discharge from war, nor will wickedness deliver those who are given to it.<sup>9</sup>All this I observed while applying my heart to all that is done under the sun, when man had power over man to his hurt.<sup>10</sup>Then I saw the wicked buried. They used to go in and out of the holy place and were praised in the city where they had done such things. This also is vanity.<sup>11</sup>Because the sentence against an evil deed is not executed speedily, the heart of the children of man is fully set to do evil.<sup>12</sup>Though a sinner does evil a hundred times and prolongs his life, yet I know that it will be well with those who fear God, because they fear before him.<sup>13</sup>But it will not be well with the wicked, neither will he prolong his days like a shadow, because he does not fear before God.<sup>14</sup>There is a vanity that takes place on earth, that there are righteous people to whom it happens according to the deeds of the wicked, and there are wicked people to whom it happens according to the deeds of the righteous. I said that this also is vanity.<sup>15</sup>And I commend joy, for man has nothing better under the sun but to eat and drink and be joyful, for this will go with him in his toil through the days of his life that God has given him under the sun.<sup>16</sup>When I applied my heart to know wisdom, and to see the business that is done on earth, how neither day nor night do one's eyes see sleep,<sup>17</sup>then I saw all the work of God, that man cannot find out the work that is done under the sun. However much man may toil in seeking, he will not find it out. Even though a wise man claims to know, he cannot find it out.
8.overview:
Wisdom makes a man's face shine (v. 1). The wise keep the king's command because of the oath before God, avoid rash departures and evil causes, and know the proper time and way, though no one knows the future (vv. 2-7). No one has power over the day of death, and the Preacher has seen man rule over man to his hurt (vv. 8-9).

The wicked are buried with honour (v. 10). Because sentence against evil is not carried out quickly, people set their hearts on evil (v. 11). Yet it will be well with those who fear God and not with the wicked (vv. 12-13), even though on earth the righteous sometimes receive what the wicked deserve (v. 14). So the Preacher commends joy (v. 15).

However much a person seeks, he cannot find out the work of God; even the wise man who claims to know cannot (vv. 16-17).
8.theology:
God ordains civil authority, and believers submit to it for his sake (vv. 2-4; Rom 13:1; 1 Pet 2:13-17), unless commanded to disobey God (Acts 5:29). No one has power over death (v. 8) except Christ, who laid down his life and took it up again (John 10:18; Heb 2:14).

God's delay in judgment is patience meant to lead to repentance, not indifference (v. 11; 2 Pet 3:9; Rom 2:4-5). It will be well with those who fear God (vv. 12-13), though the meantime is full of inversions (v. 14; Luke 16:25).

The full work of God cannot be found out by human wisdom (vv. 16-17; Job 26:14); what he has revealed is enough to live by (Deut 29:29).
8.examples:
A face made gentle by years of walking with God.

Storming out of the boss's office.

The eulogy that bore no resemblance to the life.

The fraud that goes unnoticed for years.

The shadow that lengthens just before it vanishes.

9.title: One Event for All, and Bread Eaten with Joy

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Same Event Happens to All
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The righteous and the wise are in the hand of God, though no one can read from events whether God's love or hate is on him (v. 1). It is the same for all: death comes to righteous and wicked alike, and the hearts of men are full of evil (vv. 2-3). A living dog is better than a dead lion (v. 4), for the dead have no more share in all that is done under the sun (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Circumstances cannot tell you whether God loves you; death comes to all; and life, while it lasts, is hope.

verseByVerse.quote: But all this I laid to heart, examining it all, how the righteous and the wise and their deeds are in the hand of God. Whether it is love or hate, man does not know; both are before him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But all this I laid to heart, examining it all, how the righteous and the wise and their deeds are in the hand of God. Whether it is love or hate, man does not know; both are before him.

After confessing that no one can find out the work of God (8:17), the Preacher holds on to one thing: the righteous and the wise and their deeds are in the hand of God. Their lives, and everything they do, are held by him. That is the believer's security even when nothing else is clear. Jesus said of his sheep, no one is able to snatch them out of the Father's hand (John 10:29).

But he adds a hard truth. Whether it is love or hate, man does not know from looking at what happens. You cannot read God's heart toward you from your circumstances. A promotion is not proof of his favour; a diagnosis is not proof of his anger. Both are before him: everything that lies ahead is in his view, not ours.

That is why the believer does not look to his circumstances to learn whether God loves him. He looks to the cross, where God proved it.

verseByVerse.quote: It is the same for all, since the same event happens to the righteous and the wicked, to the good and the evil, to the clean and the unclean, to him who sacrifices and him who does not sacrifice. As the good one is, so is the sinner, and he who swears is as he who shuns an oath. This is an evil in all that is done under the sun, that the same event happens to all. Also, the hearts of the children of man are full of evil, and madness is in their hearts while they live, and after that they go to the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is the same for all, since the same event happens to the righteous and the wicked, to the good and the evil, to the clean and the unclean, to him who sacrifices and him who does not sacrifice. As the good one is, so is the sinner, and he who swears is as he who shuns an oath.

The same event is death, and the Preacher lists six pairs to prove that it comes to everyone. The religious and the irreligious, the one who worships and the one who never does: the hearse comes for both. The ESV notes that and the evil comes from ancient translations; the Hebrew lacks it. The point stands without it.

This does not mean there is no difference between them. It means death does not show the difference. God makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good (Matt 5:45), and he lets the shadow of death fall on both. The difference will be shown on the other side.

This is an evil in all that is done under the sun, that the same event happens to all. Also, the hearts of the children of man are full of evil, and madness is in their hearts while they live, and after that they go to the dead.

Death is an evil. The Preacher does not pretend it is natural or friendly. And then he names a second evil, inside: the hearts of the children of man are full of evil. Here is why death comes to all. It is not arbitrary. The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick (Jer 17:9). Madness while we live, and then the grave. That is humanity without redemption.

verseByVerse.quote: But he who is joined with all the living has hope, for a living dog is better than a dead lion. For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing, and they have no more reward, for the memory of them is forgotten. Their love and their hate and their envy have already perished, and forever they have no more share in all that is done under the sun.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he who is joined with all the living has hope, for a living dog is better than a dead lion.

In Israel dogs were despised scavengers. David called himself a dead dog to show how low he was (1 Sam 24:14). Lions were the kings of beasts. Yet a living dog is better off than a dead lion, because while there is life, there is hope. The dead lion's strength is over. The dog can still eat, still bark, still change.

This is a word to anyone who feels like the dog. While you are alive, it is not too late. Not too late to repent, to be reconciled, to begin again with God. The thief on the cross had hours left, and they were enough.

For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing, and they have no more reward, for the memory of them is forgotten. Their love and their hate and their envy have already perished, and forever they have no more share in all that is done under the sun.

The living have one advantage: they know they will die, and can act on that knowledge. The dead know nothing.

Does this mean the dead are unconscious, or that the soul sleeps? Read the last phrase: they have no more share in all that is done under the sun. The Preacher is speaking of the dead in relation to this world. They know nothing of what happens here, earn nothing here, love and hate nothing here. He is not describing what lies beyond, which the New Testament makes clear. Jesus told of a poor man who died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side, and a rich man who was fully conscious in Hades (Luke 16:22-23). Paul longed to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better (Phil 1:23). Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord, that they may rest from their labors, for their deeds follow them! (Rev 14:13). Their share under the sun is over. Their life with God is not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–10 — Go, Eat Your Bread with Joy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Go, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart, for God has already approved what you do (v. 7). Wear white and oil your head (v. 8). Enjoy life with the wife whom you love (v. 9). Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might, for there is no work in Sheol (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Life is short and death is certain, so receive each day's gifts gladly and work at each day's task wholeheartedly.

verseByVerse.quote: Go, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart, for God has already approved what you do. Let your garments be always white. Let not oil be lacking on your head.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart, for God has already approved what you do.

Having looked death full in the face, the Preacher does not despair. He issues a command, and it is a command to enjoy. Go, eat your bread with joy. This is the fullest of the "nothing better" passages, and it comes right after the grimmest look at death. The shortness of life is not a reason to be gloomy; it is a reason to take each meal as a gift.

And the ground of this joy is striking: God has already approved what you do. The person who fears God does not eat his supper wondering whether God is frowning at him for enjoying it. God gave it, and God is pleased when it is received gladly. For the Christian this has a deeper root still. The believer does not work to win God's approval; he lives from it. There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:1). You can enjoy your bread tonight because the verdict on you is already in.

Let your garments be always white. Let not oil be lacking on your head.

White garments and oil were signs of celebration, the clothes of a feast rather than of mourning. You anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows (Ps 23:5). The Preacher says: live festively. Not in excess, but in gladness. And Scripture gives the image a further meaning. The risen Christ promises that his faithful people will walk with me in white (Rev 3:4). The feast begun in faith here will go on forever.

verseByVerse.quote: Enjoy life with the wife whom you love, all the days of your vain life that he has given you under the sun, because that is your portion in life and in your toil at which you toil under the sun.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Enjoy life with the wife whom you love, all the days of your vain life that he has given you under the sun, because that is your portion in life and in your toil at which you toil under the sun.

Marriage is one of God's best gifts in a breath-like life, and the ESV's note marks vain as hebel again. Life is short; so do not waste it in coldness toward your spouse. Enjoy life with the wife whom you love. Proverbs says the same: rejoice in the wife of your youth (Prov 5:18).

Notice the phrase your portion. Your spouse is part of the share God has given you. Not the fantasy someone else, not the life you might have had, but this person. Many marriages are poisoned by comparison. The Preacher calls you to delight in your portion. And for Christians the pattern is set higher still: Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Eph 5:25).

When did you last simply enjoy your husband or wife, not as a partner in logistics, but as God's gift?

verseByVerse.quote: Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might, for there is no work or thought or knowledge or wisdom in Sheol, to which you are going.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might, for there is no work or thought or knowledge or wisdom in Sheol, to which you are going.

Joy in the gifts, and energy in the work. Whatever your hand finds to do: the task in front of you, whatever it is. Do it with your might: not half-heartedly, not waiting for a more important job. The ESV notes a possible rendering, "finds to do with your might, do it", but either way the call is wholehearted work.

The reason is the grave. Sheol, the realm of the dead, is where there is no work. The time for this world's work is now. Jesus said, We must work the works of him who sent me while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work (John 9:4).

For the believer this is doubled. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men (Col 3:23). The dishes, the spreadsheet, the lesson plan, the hospital shift: do it with your might, as service to Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, but time and chance happen to them all (v. 11). Like fish in a net and birds in a snare, people are caught by an evil time that falls suddenly (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Ability does not guarantee outcomes; only God holds the times.

verseByVerse.quote: Again I saw that under the sun the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor bread to the wise, nor riches to the intelligent, nor favor to those with knowledge, but time and chance happen to them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again I saw that under the sun the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor bread to the wise, nor riches to the intelligent, nor favor to those with knowledge, but time and chance happen to them all.

Five things we expect: the fastest runner wins, the strongest army wins, the wise earn their bread, the clever get rich, the skilled get recognised. Usually, perhaps. Not always. The favourite stumbles. The brilliant graduate cannot find work. The talented go unnoticed.

Time and chance happen to them all. From under the sun, it looks like chance: the wrong place, the wrong moment. Scripture shows what lies behind it. The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD (Prov 16:33). The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD (Prov 21:31). What looks like chance to us is not chance to God. Not one sparrow will fall to the ground apart from your Father (Matt 10:29).

That frees us from two errors: pride when we win, as if our ability guaranteed it, and bitterness when we lose, as if no one were in control.

verseByVerse.quote: For man does not know his time. Like fish that are taken in an evil net, and like birds that are caught in a snare, so the children of man are snared at an evil time, when it suddenly falls upon them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For man does not know his time. Like fish that are taken in an evil net, and like birds that are caught in a snare, so the children of man are snared at an evil time, when it suddenly falls upon them.

The fish swims into the net without seeing it. The bird hops toward the bait. Neither knows that this is the moment. Man does not know his time: the accident, the heart attack, the collapse of the firm, the day of death.

Jesus used the same picture for the end of the age. In Noah's day They were eating and drinking and marrying and being given in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all (Luke 17:27). Therefore you also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect (Matt 24:44). The only preparation for an unknown hour is to be ready at every hour.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–18 — The Poor Wise Man Who Saved the City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A great king besieged a little city, and a poor, wise man delivered it by his wisdom, Yet no one remembered that poor man (vv. 13-15). Wisdom is better than might, though the poor man's words are despised (v. 16). Quiet words of the wise are better than a ruler's shouting, Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner destroys much good (vv. 17-18).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom saves more than strength, and the world rarely thanks the one who saved it.

verseByVerse.quote: I have also seen this example of wisdom under the sun, and it seemed great to me. There was a little city with few men in it, and a great king came against it and besieged it, building great siegeworks against it. But there was found in it a poor, wise man, and he by his wisdom delivered the city. Yet no one remembered that poor man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have also seen this example of wisdom under the sun, and it seemed great to me.

The Preacher tells a parable, perhaps something he actually saw, and calls it great.

There was a little city with few men in it, and a great king came against it and besieged it, building great siegeworks against it. But there was found in it a poor, wise man, and he by his wisdom delivered the city. Yet no one remembered that poor man.

A little city, a great king, great siegeworks: hopeless odds. And the rescuer is not a general but a poor man with wisdom. Scripture has a real example: when Joab besieged the town of Abel, a wise woman called from the city, and the woman went to all the people in her wisdom, and the city was spared (2 Sam 20:16, 22).

Then the sting: no one remembered that poor man. The city was saved, and the saviour was forgotten. The people who do the most good are often the least honoured.

It is hard to read this story without thinking of another poor man. Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor (2 Cor 8:9). He came to a world under siege by death and delivered it, and he was despised and rejected by men (Isa 53:3). The Preacher did not have him in view. But the pattern he saw is the pattern of the gospel: God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong (1 Cor 1:27). The difference is that this poor man will not be forgotten. God has given him the name above every name.

verseByVerse.quote: But I say that wisdom is better than might, though the poor man's wisdom is despised and his words are not heard. The words of the wise heard in quiet are better than the shouting of a ruler among fools. Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner destroys much good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I say that wisdom is better than might, though the poor man's wisdom is despised and his words are not heard.

The moral: wisdom beats force. And yet people rarely listen to the poor. If a wise idea comes from someone without status, it is ignored; if a foolish one comes from someone important, it is applauded. That tells you something about us, not about wisdom.

The words of the wise heard in quiet are better than the shouting of a ruler among fools.

Loudness is not authority. The quiet counsel of a wise person, given calmly and heard in stillness, does more good than a ruler shouting at a room full of fools. Listen for the quiet voices.

Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner destroys much good.

Two truths side by side. Wisdom is stronger than weapons. And one sinner can undo it. One poor man saved a city; one fool could lose it. Achan's single act of theft brought defeat on all Israel (Josh 7:1). Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump? (1 Cor 5:6). It takes a lifetime to build what one act of folly can destroy, and the next chapter opens with the same warning.

9.text: <sup>1</sup>But all this I laid to heart, examining it all, how the righteous and the wise and their deeds are in the hand of God. Whether it is love or hate, man does not know; both are before him.<sup>2</sup>It is the same for all, since the same event happens to the righteous and the wicked, to the good and the evil, to the clean and the unclean, to him who sacrifices and him who does not sacrifice. As the good one is, so is the sinner, and he who swears is as he who shuns an oath.<sup>3</sup>This is an evil in all that is done under the sun, that the same event happens to all. Also, the hearts of the children of man are full of evil, and madness is in their hearts while they live, and after that they go to the dead.<sup>4</sup>But he who is joined with all the living has hope, for a living dog is better than a dead lion.<sup>5</sup>For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing, and they have no more reward, for the memory of them is forgotten.<sup>6</sup>Their love and their hate and their envy have already perished, and forever they have no more share in all that is done under the sun.<sup>7</sup>Go, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart, for God has already approved what you do.<sup>8</sup>Let your garments be always white. Let not oil be lacking on your head.<sup>9</sup>Enjoy life with the wife whom you love, all the days of your vain life that he has given you under the sun, because that is your portion in life and in your toil at which you toil under the sun.<sup>10</sup>Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might, for there is no work or thought or knowledge or wisdom in Sheol, to which you are going.<sup>11</sup>Again I saw that under the sun the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor bread to the wise, nor riches to the intelligent, nor favor to those with knowledge, but time and chance happen to them all.<sup>12</sup>For man does not know his time. Like fish that are taken in an evil net, and like birds that are caught in a snare, so the children of man are snared at an evil time, when it suddenly falls upon them.<sup>13</sup>I have also seen this example of wisdom under the sun, and it seemed great to me.<sup>14</sup>There was a little city with few men in it, and a great king came against it and besieged it, building great siegeworks against it.<sup>15</sup>But there was found in it a poor, wise man, and he by his wisdom delivered the city. Yet no one remembered that poor man.<sup>16</sup>But I say that wisdom is better than might, though the poor man's wisdom is despised and his words are not heard.<sup>17</sup>The words of the wise heard in quiet are better than the shouting of a ruler among fools.<sup>18</sup>Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner destroys much good.
9.overview:
The righteous and the wise are in God's hand, but no one can tell from events whether God's love or hate is upon him (v. 1). The same event, death, comes to righteous and wicked alike, and human hearts are full of evil (vv. 2-3). Yet a living dog is better than a dead lion, for the dead have no more share in what is done under the sun (vv. 4-6).

So the Preacher commands joy: eat bread with joy and drink wine gladly, for God has approved; wear white; enjoy life with the wife you love; and do with your might whatever your hand finds to do, for there is no work in Sheol (vv. 7-10).

The race is not to the swift nor the battle to the strong; time and chance happen to all, and people are caught by evil times like fish in a net (vv. 11-12). A poor, wise man delivered a besieged city and was forgotten; wisdom is better than might and weapons, but one sinner destroys much good (vv. 13-18).
9.theology:
God's people are in his hand (v. 1; John 10:29), but his love cannot be read from circumstances. Death comes to all because human hearts are evil (vv. 2-3; Jer 17:9). The dead have no share in this world (vv. 5-6), but those who die in the Lord are with him (Luke 16:22; Phil 1:23; Rev 14:13).

Joy in God's gifts and wholehearted work are commanded, grounded in God's approval (vv. 7-10); for believers that approval rests on Christ (Rom 8:1). What seems chance is governed by God (v. 11; Prov 16:33; Matt 10:29). Wisdom saves, yet the world forgets its deliverers (vv. 13-15), a pattern fulfilled in Christ, who became poor to make many rich (2 Cor 8:9).
9.examples:
A promotion is not proof of God's favour, nor a diagnosis of his anger.

The hearse comes for the worshipper and the scoffer alike.

Tonight's supper eaten without wondering whether God is frowning.

The brilliant graduate who cannot find work.

The fish that swims into the net.

The quiet voice in the meeting that no one hears.

10.title: Dead Flies and Sharp Iron

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — A Little Folly, and Folly in High Places
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Dead flies make the perfumer's ointment give off a stench; so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor (v. 1). The wise heart and the fool's heart go different ways, and the fool shows it on the road (vv. 2-3). When a ruler is angry, stay calm (v. 4). The Preacher has seen folly promoted and nobles humbled: slaves on horses, and princes walking on the ground like slaves (vv. 5-7).
verseByVerse.theology: A little folly spoils much, and a world where folly rules is a world turned upside down.

verseByVerse.quote: Dead flies make the perfumer's ointment give off a stench; so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dead flies make the perfumer's ointment give off a stench; so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor.

Chapter 9 ended, one sinner destroys much good. Chapter 10 opens with a picture of the same truth. A jar of expensive perfume, made with care, and a few flies get in and die. Soon the whole jar stinks. It does not take much folly to ruin a great deal of wisdom.

A pastor with thirty years of faithful ministry and one affair. A businessman known for integrity and one fraudulent signature. A father who was patient for years and one explosion of rage that his child never forgets. Reputation takes a lifetime to build, and a little folly outweighs it.

That is a sobering word, and it calls for watchfulness over small things. The flies were small. Which small compromise are you tolerating because it seems too minor to matter?

verseByVerse.quote: A wise man's heart inclines him to the right, but a fool's heart to the left. Even when the fool walks on the road, he lacks sense, and he says to everyone that he is a fool.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wise man's heart inclines him to the right, but a fool's heart to the left.

The right hand in Scripture is the hand of strength and favour, the left the weaker side. The saying has nothing to do with modern politics. It means the wise man's heart pulls him toward what is good and skilful, and the fool's pulls him the other way. Everyone's heart leans somewhere, and the lean decides the direction of the life.

Even when the fool walks on the road, he lacks sense, and he says to everyone that he is a fool.

A fool does not need to announce his folly. He simply walks down the road, and everyone can see it. The way he speaks, the way he treats people, the decisions he makes in plain view: he says to everyone that he is a fool. A fool's mouth is his ruin (Prov 18:7). Character leaks out in ordinary moments.

verseByVerse.quote: If the anger of the ruler rises against you, do not leave your place, for calmness will lay great offenses to rest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the anger of the ruler rises against you, do not leave your place, for calmness will lay great offenses to rest.

Practical counsel for anyone with a boss. When the person over you is angry, the instinct is to storm out, quit, or hit back. Do not leave your place. Stay steady. The ESV notes that calmness is in Hebrew "healing". A calm response heals. It can put great offenses to rest.

A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger (Prov 15:1). With patience a ruler may be persuaded, and a soft tongue will break a bone (Prov 25:15). This is not cowardice. It takes more strength to stay calm under someone's anger than to return it.

verseByVerse.quote: There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, as it were an error proceeding from the ruler: folly is set in many high places, and the rich sit in a low place. I have seen slaves on horses, and princes walking on the ground like slaves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, as it were an error proceeding from the ruler: folly is set in many high places, and the rich sit in a low place.

Now the problem is at the top. A ruler makes bad appointments. Fools get the high offices, and capable people are pushed aside. The Preacher calls it an error, as if it were a mistake, and it has the effects of a disaster.

I have seen slaves on horses, and princes walking on the ground like slaves.

A world upside down. The ones fit to lead walk, and the ones unfit ride. Isaiah pronounced it as a judgment: I will make boys their princes, and infants shall rule over them (Isa 3:4). When leadership goes to the unworthy, a society suffers.

But notice what Jesus did with the upside-down world. He was the Prince of all, and he walked on the ground. He rode into Jerusalem not on a warhorse but on a donkey. For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). The reversal the Preacher lamented, Christ chose, and by it he turned the world right side up.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — Risks, Sharp Tools and the Fool's Tongue
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every task has its hazard: the pit, the wall, the stones, the logs (vv. 8-9). If the iron is blunt more strength is needed, but wisdom helps one to succeed (vv. 10-11). The words of a wise man's mouth win him favor, but the lips of a fool consume him; the fool multiplies words about a future he cannot know (vv. 12-14), and his toil wears him out because he does not know the way to the city (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom sharpens the edge of ordinary work and guards the tongue.

verseByVerse.quote: He who digs a pit will fall into it, and a serpent will bite him who breaks through a wall. He who quarries stones is hurt by them, and he who splits logs is endangered by them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who digs a pit will fall into it, and a serpent will bite him who breaks through a wall.

These verses are about the risks built into every activity. The man who digs a pit may fall into it; the man who breaks through an old stone wall disturbs the snake living in it. Scripture often uses the pit as a picture of wickedness recoiling on itself: Whoever digs a pit will fall into it (Prov 26:27), and Haman was hanged on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai (Esth 7:10). But here the point seems wider. Every job has its danger.

He who quarries stones is hurt by them, and he who splits logs is endangered by them.

The quarryman gets crushed fingers; the woodcutter a flying splinter or a slipped axe. The work itself carries risk. That is not a reason to refuse work. It is a reason to do it wisely, with care, and not to be surprised when ordinary life has hazards. Wisdom does not remove all risk. It reduces it.

verseByVerse.quote: If the iron is blunt, and one does not sharpen the edge, he must use more strength, but wisdom helps one to succeed. If the serpent bites before it is charmed, there is no advantage to the charmer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the iron is blunt, and one does not sharpen the edge, he must use more strength, but wisdom helps one to succeed.

Anyone who has cut wood with a dull axe knows this verse. You swing harder, sweat more, and get less done. Stop, sharpen the blade, and the work goes quickly. The ESV notes that the last line may be rendered "wisdom is an advantage for success". Wisdom is the sharpening.

Many people are working harder and harder with a blunt edge: busier, more tired, less effective. The wise thing is sometimes to stop swinging. Rest, pray, learn, plan, ask advice. Time spent sharpening is not time lost.

If the serpent bites before it is charmed, there is no advantage to the charmer.

Skill must be used at the right time. The snake charmer who arrives a moment late has no advantage over anyone else. Wisdom that is not applied when it is needed is useless. The right word tomorrow does not help today.

verseByVerse.quote: The words of a wise man's mouth win him favor, but the lips of a fool consume him. The beginning of the words of his mouth is foolishness, and the end of his talk is evil madness. A fool multiplies words, though no man knows what is to be, and who can tell him what will be after him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The words of a wise man's mouth win him favor, but the lips of a fool consume him.

The ESV notes that win him favor may be rendered "are gracious". The wise man's words are gracious, and grace wins favour. The fool's words consume him: he talks himself into trouble. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt (Col 4:6).

The beginning of the words of his mouth is foolishness, and the end of his talk is evil madness.

A fool's speech gets worse the longer it goes on. He starts with nonsense and ends in madness. When words are many, transgression is not lacking (Prov 10:19). Anyone who has watched an argument escalate has seen it.

A fool multiplies words, though no man knows what is to be, and who can tell him what will be after him?

The fool talks endlessly about the future as if he knew it: the predictions, the plans, the confident forecasts. But no one knows what is to be. James calls the tongue a fire (Jas 3:6), and Jesus warned that on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak (Matt 12:36). How many of your words this week were about things you could not possibly know?

verseByVerse.quote: The toil of a fool wearies him, for he does not know the way to the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The toil of a fool wearies him, for he does not know the way to the city.

A vivid and slightly comic picture. The fool works hard and wears himself out, and he cannot even find the road into town. All that effort, and he is lost on the obvious path.

Energy without direction exhausts. It is possible to be busy all day and get nowhere because you never asked where you were going. For the Christian, the way to the city is not hidden. The one who said I am the way is the road to the city that is to come (Heb 13:14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–20 — Kings, Sloth, Money and the Whispered Curse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Woe to you, O land, when your king is a child and princes feast in the morning; happy the land whose princes feast for strength, and not for drunkenness (vv. 16-17). Sloth brings the roof down (v. 18). Bread, wine and money each have their use (v. 19). Even in your thoughts, do not curse the king, for a bird of the air will carry your voice (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: Self-control in those who lead, diligence in those who work, and restraint in what we say in private.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you, O land, when your king is a child, and your princes feast in the morning! Happy are you, O land, when your king is the son of the nobility, and your princes feast at the proper time, for strength, and not for drunkenness!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, O land, when your king is a child, and your princes feast in the morning!

A nation in trouble: a king who is immature, whether in years or in character, and officials who start drinking at breakfast. Woe to those who rise early in the morning, that they may run after strong drink (Isa 5:11). When leaders indulge themselves, the people pay.

Happy are you, O land, when your king is the son of the nobility, and your princes feast at the proper time, for strength, and not for drunkenness!

And a nation blessed: a king of noble character, and officials who eat and drink at the right time, for strength, and not for drunkenness. Feasting is not wrong; eating is for strength. But It is not for kings to drink wine, lest they drink and forget what has been decreed (Prov 31:4-5). Self-control in leaders is a blessing to a whole people. The same applies to anyone who leads a family, a team or a church. Do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit (Eph 5:18).

verseByVerse.quote: Through sloth the roof sinks in, and through indolence the house leaks. Bread is made for laughter, and wine gladdens life, and money answers everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through sloth the roof sinks in, and through indolence the house leaks.

No single moment brings the roof down. A tile slips and is not replaced. Water gets in. The beam rots. Years later the ceiling collapses. Sloth works slowly, and its results arrive suddenly. The sluggard's vineyard in Proverbs was all overgrown with thorns, and its stone wall was broken down (Prov 24:31).

This is true of houses, and of nations, and of marriages and souls. The neglected prayer life, the unaddressed conflict, the small repair put off: the roof sinks in.

Bread is made for laughter, and wine gladdens life, and money answers everything.

Read in context, this sounds like the careless princes speaking: feast, drink, and money will cover it. It is also, in part, simply true. Food and wine are for joy, and money does solve many practical problems. But the book has already shown what money cannot answer: He who loves money will not be satisfied with money (5:10), and it cannot buy the power to enjoy (6:2). Money answers everything except the questions that matter most.

verseByVerse.quote: Even in your thoughts, do not curse the king, nor in your bedroom curse the rich, for a bird of the air will carry your voice, or some winged creature tell the matter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even in your thoughts, do not curse the king, nor in your bedroom curse the rich, for a bird of the air will carry your voice, or some winged creature tell the matter.

It sounds like the old saying, "a little bird told me". Words spoken in private have a way of getting out. The complaint about the boss in the car, the message you thought was private, the joke told behind a closed door: a bird of the air will carry your voice.

But the verse goes deeper than prudence. Even in your thoughts. The curse begins in the heart before it reaches the lips. Scripture commands honour for those in authority: You shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler of your people (Exod 22:28). This does not forbid honest criticism or opposition to injustice. It forbids the private contempt that poisons the one who nurses it.

And there is one listener no one can hide from. Jesus said, whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light (Luke 12:3). Speak in private as you would if the one you speak of were in the room, because the one who judges all things always is.
