10.overview:
A little folly outweighs wisdom, as dead flies spoil perfume (v. 1). The wise and the fool lean different ways, and the fool shows himself on the road (vv. 2-3). When a ruler is angry, calmness settles great offences (v. 4). The Preacher has seen folly in high places, slaves on horses and princes on foot (vv. 5-7).

Every task has its risks (vv. 8-9); a blunt axe needs more strength, but wisdom brings success, and skill must be used in time (vv. 10-11). A wise man's words are gracious, but a fool's words consume him, grow worse as they go, and presume on a future no one knows (vv. 12-14). The fool's toil wears him out, and he cannot find the way to the city (v. 15).

A land is cursed when its king is childish and its princes drink in the morning, and blessed when its leaders feast for strength (vv. 16-17). Sloth brings the roof down (v. 18). Bread, wine and money have their uses (v. 19). Do not curse the king even in private, for a bird will carry the words (v. 20).
10.theology:
Small sins do great damage (v. 1; 1 Cor 5:6), and character shows in ordinary conduct (v. 3). Calm, gracious speech heals and persuades (vv. 4, 12; Prov 15:1; Col 4:6); careless words will be judged (Matt 12:36).

Wisdom does not remove risk but makes work effective (vv. 8-11). Leaders are to exercise self-control for the good of the people (vv. 16-17; Prov 31:4-5), and those under authority are to honour them, even in thought (v. 20; Exod 22:28). Christ, the Prince who walked as a servant, overturns the world's disordered rule (vv. 5-7; Mark 10:45).
10.examples:
Thirty years of faithful ministry and one affair.

Staying calm when the boss is shouting.

Swinging a dull axe harder instead of stopping to sharpen it.

The argument that begins in nonsense and ends in madness.

The loose tile that brings down the ceiling years later.

The complaint in the car that somehow reaches the boss.

11.title: Cast Your Bread upon the Waters

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Cast Your Bread, Sow Your Seed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Cast your bread upon the waters, for you will find it after many days; give generously, for no one knows what disaster may come (vv. 1-2). What will happen will happen, and He who observes the wind will not sow (vv. 3-4). No one knows the work of God (v. 5), so In the morning sow your seed, and at evening withhold not your hand (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Uncertainty about the future is a reason for generosity and diligence, not for hoarding and hesitation.

verseByVerse.quote: Cast your bread upon the waters, for you will find it after many days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cast your bread upon the waters, for you will find it after many days.

The book's final section turns from observation to action. After ten chapters of uncertainty, you might expect the Preacher to say: since you cannot know the future, hold on tight to what you have. He says the opposite. Let it go.

The picture is of throwing bread onto water, which looks like pure waste. It floats away. But you will find it after many days. Many take it as a picture of generosity: what is given freely comes back. Others see sea trade, sending goods out on ships and waiting for the return. Either way, the principle is the same: the person who holds everything close never sees a harvest. Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him (Prov 19:17). One gives freely, yet grows all the richer (Prov 11:24).

Jesus put it at its fullest: give, and it will be given to you. Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over (Luke 6:38). The return may take many days. Some of it may come only in eternity. But nothing given in faith is lost.

verseByVerse.quote: Give a portion to seven, or even to eight, for you know not what disaster may happen on earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give a portion to seven, or even to eight, for you know not what disaster may happen on earth.

Be generous widely: seven, even eight. The reason given is surprising: you know not what disaster may happen. The worldly reasoning is, disaster may come, so hoard. The Preacher's reasoning is, disaster may come, so give while you can. Tomorrow you may have nothing to give, or you may need the friends your generosity made.

It also reads as prudent advice about spreading risk: do not put everything in one place. Both senses fit a world where no one knows what is coming. Jesus said, make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth, so that when it fails they may receive you into the eternal dwellings (Luke 16:9). Money will fail. Use it now in ways that last.

verseByVerse.quote: If the clouds are full of rain, they empty themselves on the earth, and if a tree falls to the south or to the north, in the place where the tree falls, there it will lie. He who observes the wind will not sow, and he who regards the clouds will not reap.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the clouds are full of rain, they empty themselves on the earth, and if a tree falls to the south or to the north, in the place where the tree falls, there it will lie.

Some things are beyond our control. Full clouds will rain. A tree falls where it falls. You cannot argue with the weather or pick up a fallen oak by wishing. What will happen, will happen.

He who observes the wind will not sow, and he who regards the clouds will not reap.

So do not wait for perfect conditions. The farmer who stands watching the wind, waiting for the ideal day to sow, never sows. The one who keeps checking the clouds for rain never brings in the harvest. There is always a reason to wait.

This is a word for the perfectionist and the procrastinator. The right time to start the business, have the conversation, share the gospel with your neighbour, begin giving, apply for the job, will never look perfect. Let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up (Gal 6:9). What are you waiting on the wind for?

verseByVerse.quote: As you do not know the way the spirit comes to the bones in the womb of a woman with child, so you do not know the work of God who makes everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As you do not know the way the spirit comes to the bones in the womb of a woman with child, so you do not know the work of God who makes everything.

The ESV notes that most Hebrew manuscripts read, "As you do not know the way of the wind, or how the bones grow in the womb". Either way, the verse sets two mysteries side by side. No one can explain how life forms in the womb, how breath and bone become a person. And no one can explain the work of God who makes everything.

Modern medicine can describe the stages of a baby's growth in detail, and still marvel at it. The psalmist worshipped: you knitted me together in my mother's womb. I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made (Ps 139:13-14). Jesus used the wind to describe the new birth: The wind blows where it wishes, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes (John 3:8).

The point for daily life is humility. You do not understand how God works, so you cannot calculate the outcome of your sowing. That is not a reason to stop. It is a reason to trust the one who does understand.

verseByVerse.quote: In the morning sow your seed, and at evening withhold not your hand, for you do not know which will prosper, this or that, or whether both alike will be good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the morning sow your seed, and at evening withhold not your hand, for you do not know which will prosper, this or that, or whether both alike will be good.

Here is the conclusion of the first half of the chapter. Since you cannot know which effort will succeed, work morning and evening. Sow widely. Some seed will fail; some will flourish; perhaps both.

This is the principle of every faithful ministry, parent and worker. You teach the Sunday school class, raise your children, pray for your friends, do your job well, and you do not know which of it God will make fruitful. Jesus said the kingdom is like a man who scatters seed: He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how (Mark 4:27). Paul said, I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth (1 Cor 3:6). Sow; God gives the growth. That frees you from the need to see results, and from the despair of not seeing them yet.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Light is sweet (v. 7). Rejoice in all your years, but remember that the days of darkness will be many (v. 8). Rejoice, O young man, in your youth, But know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment (v. 9). Put away vexation and pain, for youth and the dawn of life are vanity (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Joy and accountability belong together; youth is to be enjoyed before God, because it will not last.

verseByVerse.quote: Light is sweet, and it is pleasant for the eyes to see the sun. So if a person lives many years, let him rejoice in them all; but let him remember that the days of darkness will be many. All that comes is vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Light is sweet, and it is pleasant for the eyes to see the sun.

After so much about the sun as the ceiling over a weary world, here the sun is simply lovely. Light is sweet. The morning light through a window, a warm day, the sight of the sun on water: these are pleasures from God, and the Preacher wants us to feel them. This is the day that the LORD has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it (Ps 118:24).

So if a person lives many years, let him rejoice in them all; but let him remember that the days of darkness will be many. All that comes is vanity.

Two commands held together. Rejoice in them all: every year, not only the good ones. And remember that darkness is coming, the days of old age and death. The remembering is not meant to spoil the joy. It is meant to make it urgent. Enjoy the light because it will not last. All that comes is vanity, as the ESV's note marks it: breath.

People who never think about death tend to waste their days. People who think about nothing else tend to waste them too. The Preacher asks for both at once: gladness, and a clear eye.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice, O young man, in your youth, and let your heart cheer you in the days of your youth. Walk in the ways of your heart and the sight of your eyes. But know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejoice, O young man, in your youth, and let your heart cheer you in the days of your youth. Walk in the ways of your heart and the sight of your eyes.

Now he speaks directly to the young. And his first word is not "be careful" but Rejoice. Youth is a gift. Let your heart be glad. Follow the good desires of your heart, enjoy what your eyes see. God is not the enemy of youthful energy, adventure and delight.

Is that not dangerous? Moses warned Israel not to follow after your own heart and your own eyes (Num 15:39). The difference is in the next sentence, which governs everything before it.

But know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment.

Enjoy your youth, and know that you will give account for how you enjoyed it. This is not a threat that cancels the joy. It is what makes the joy safe. The young person who knows he will stand before God will enjoy life in ways he will not be ashamed of. So then each of us will give an account of himself to God (Rom 14:12). So flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace (2 Tim 2:22).

Joy without judgment becomes licence. Judgment without joy becomes grim religion. The Preacher holds them together, and so should every parent, youth leader and young believer.

verseByVerse.quote: Remove vexation from your heart, and put away pain from your body, for youth and the dawn of life are vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remove vexation from your heart, and put away pain from your body, for youth and the dawn of life are vanity.

Get rid of what spoils youth: the anxieties that eat at the heart, the self-inflicted pains of the body. The ESV notes that pain may be rendered "evil": put away evil from your body, the sins that damage it. Do not waste the strength of youth on worry or on vice.

Why? For youth and the dawn of life are vanity. Hebel again, breath. Not worthless, but fleeting. Youth passes faster than anyone at twenty can believe. The glory of young men is their strength (Prov 20:29), and strength does not last.

This leads straight into the great poem of chapter 12, and its first word: Remember. The best use of a fleeting youth is to give it to the God who will not pass away. It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth (Lam 3:27).

11.text: <sup>1</sup>Cast your bread upon the waters, for you will find it after many days.<sup>2</sup>Give a portion to seven, or even to eight, for you know not what disaster may happen on earth.<sup>3</sup>If the clouds are full of rain, they empty themselves on the earth, and if a tree falls to the south or to the north, in the place where the tree falls, there it will lie.<sup>4</sup>He who observes the wind will not sow, and he who regards the clouds will not reap.<sup>5</sup>As you do not know the way the spirit comes to the bones in the womb of a woman with child, so you do not know the work of God who makes everything.<sup>6</sup>In the morning sow your seed, and at evening withhold not your hand, for you do not know which will prosper, this or that, or whether both alike will be good.<sup>7</sup>Light is sweet, and it is pleasant for the eyes to see the sun.<sup>8</sup>So if a person lives many years, let him rejoice in them all; but let him remember that the days of darkness will be many. All that comes is vanity.<sup>9</sup>Rejoice, O young man, in your youth, and let your heart cheer you in the days of your youth. Walk in the ways of your heart and the sight of your eyes. But know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment.<sup>10</sup>Remove vexation from your heart, and put away pain from your body, for youth and the dawn of life are vanity.
11.overview:
The Preacher calls for bold generosity and diligence in an uncertain world. Cast your bread upon the waters, for you will find it after many days, and give to seven or eight, since no one knows what disaster may come (vv. 1-2). Clouds rain and trees fall where they will, but the one who watches the wind will never sow (vv. 3-4). As no one understands how life forms in the womb, no one knows the work of God (v. 5). So sow morning and evening, not knowing which will prosper (v. 6).

Light is sweet. A person should rejoice in all his years, remembering that the days of darkness will be many (vv. 7-8). The young man is to rejoice in his youth and follow his heart, knowing that God will bring him into judgment for all of it (v. 9). He should put away vexation and evil, for youth is fleeting (v. 10).
11.theology:
Uncertainty about the future calls for generosity and diligence rather than hoarding and delay (vv. 1-6; Luke 6:38; Gal 6:9). God's work, like the forming of a child in the womb, is beyond human understanding (v. 5; Ps 139:13-14); we sow and God gives the growth (1 Cor 3:6-7).

Joy in life is commanded, and so is remembrance of death and judgment (vv. 7-9). Every person will give account to God for how he used his youth and his gifts (v. 9; Rom 14:12; 2 Cor 5:10). Youth is fleeting and best given to God (v. 10; Lam 3:27).
11.examples:
Bread thrown on the water that comes back after many days.

The farmer who keeps checking the wind and never sows.

The Sunday school class whose fruit you may never see.

Morning light through a window.

A twenty-year-old who cannot believe how fast youth goes.

12.title: Remember Your Creator: The End of the Matter

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Remember Your Creator Before the Evil Days
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come (v. 1): before the lights darken (v. 2), the body's house trembles and its windows dim (vv. 3-4), fears multiply and desire fails, because man is going to his eternal home (v. 5); before the silver cord snaps, and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it (vv. 6-7). Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher; all is vanity (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole of life, from youth to the grave, is to be lived in remembrance of the God who made it and to whom the spirit returns.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come and the years draw near of which you will say, "I have no pleasure in them";
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come and the years draw near of which you will say, "I have no pleasure in them";

Chapter 11 told the young man to rejoice. Chapter 12 continues the same sentence, joined by also: rejoice, and remember also your Creator. The two belong together. Joy is safest and deepest when it is received from the one who made you.

Remember in Scripture means more than recalling a fact. It means to keep in mind and act on. God "remembered" Noah and sent the wind; Israel was told to remember the Sabbath and keep it. To remember your Creator is to live in the constant awareness that you are his creature, that he made you, owns you, and has a claim on your days.

And notice the word Creator. After eleven chapters of "God", the Preacher chooses a word that reaches back to creation. The one who formed man from the dust (Gen 2:7) is the one to remember before you return to it (v. 7). Everything under the sun is breath. The Creator is not under the sun.

In the days of your youth: now. Not when you have settled down, made your money or had your fun. The reason is urgent. The evil days are coming, the years of age and decline of which you will say, "I have no pleasure in them". The habits of a lifetime are set early. Those who give their youth to God have a lifetime of walking with him to draw on when strength fails. O God, from my youth you have taught me, So even to old age and gray hairs, O God, do not forsake me (Ps 71:17-18). Timothy knew the Scriptures from childhood (2 Tim 3:15).

If you are young, this verse is addressed to you by name. If you are not, the day to remember your Creator is still today. The only time it will be too late is after verse 7.

verseByVerse.quote: before the sun and the light and the moon and the stars are darkened and the clouds return after the rain,
verseByVerse.commentary:
before the sun and the light and the moon and the stars are darkened and the clouds return after the rain,

The Preacher now paints old age, and he begins with a darkening sky. In youth, after a storm, the sun comes out. In age, the clouds return after the rain: one trouble follows another without a break. The lights of life dim, the eyes, the mind, the joys, one after another.

The picture may also carry a hint of something larger. Scripture uses the darkening of sun, moon and stars for the end of a world. For every person, death is the end of his world. But the main point is tender and personal: the brightness fades.

For the believer, there is a light that does not. Even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you (Isa 46:4).

verseByVerse.quote: in the day when the keepers of the house tremble, and the strong men are bent, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those who look through the windows are dimmed, and the doors on the street are shut—when the sound of the grinding is low, and one rises up at the sound of a bird, and all the daughters of song are brought low—
verseByVerse.commentary:
in the day when the keepers of the house tremble, and the strong men are bent, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those who look through the windows are dimmed,

Now the body is pictured as a great house falling into decay. Most readers have taken each image as a part of the ageing body, and the fit is striking. The keepers of the house tremble: the arms and hands that once protected it shake. The strong men are bent: the legs and back that carried it are stooped. The grinders cease because they are few: the teeth are going. Those who look through the windows are dimmed: the eyes grow weak.

and the doors on the street are shut—when the sound of the grinding is low, and one rises up at the sound of a bird, and all the daughters of song are brought low—

The doors on the street are shut: the old person goes out less, and the world grows smaller; perhaps also the ears close. The sound of the grinding is low: the mill of daily life, and of the mouth, is quiet. One rises up at the sound of a bird: sleep is light, and the old wake at dawn with the birds. All the daughters of song are brought low: the voice weakens, and music is hard to hear.

Anyone who has cared for an ageing parent recognises every line. The Preacher does not write this to mock the old. He writes it so that the young will see where the road goes, and so that the old will know God has seen what they are going through and put it in his book.

verseByVerse.quote: they are afraid also of what is high, and terrors are in the way; the almond tree blossoms, the grasshopper drags itself along, and desire fails, because man is going to his eternal home, and the mourners go about the streets—
verseByVerse.commentary:
they are afraid also of what is high, and terrors are in the way; the almond tree blossoms, the grasshopper drags itself along, and desire fails, because man is going to his eternal home, and the mourners go about the streets—

Fear of heights and falls; the street that once was easy is full of terrors: steps, traffic, crowds. The almond tree blossoms: its blossom is white, and many see the white hair of age. The grasshopper drags itself along: the creature made for leaping can barely move. The ESV notes that this may be rendered "is a burden": even something as light as a grasshopper becomes heavy. Desire fails: appetite, ambition and longing fade.

And the reason: man is going to his eternal home. Here, in the middle of a poem about decay, is a phrase full of meaning. The body's house is failing because its occupant is moving house. The grave is called a home, and an eternal one. Meanwhile the mourners go about the streets, already waiting.

Paul saw the same decay and said something the Preacher could not: Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day (2 Cor 4:16). For we know that if the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens (2 Cor 5:1). For the believer the eternal home is not the grave, but the Father's house.

verseByVerse.quote: before the silver cord is snapped, or the golden bowl is broken, or the pitcher is shattered at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern, and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
before the silver cord is snapped, or the golden bowl is broken, or the pitcher is shattered at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern,

Four pictures of the moment of death. A golden lamp bowl hangs by a silver cord; the cord snaps, the bowl falls and breaks, and the light goes out. A pitcher is carried to the spring and shatters. The wheel that draws water from the well breaks, and no more water comes up. Precious things, silver and gold, and ordinary things, pitcher and wheel: death breaks both. Life, which drew water and gave light, stops.

And each is sudden. A cord does not fray slowly in the picture; it snaps.

and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it.

Here the creation story runs backward. In Genesis, the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life (Gen 2:7). At death the two part again. The dust returns to the earth: for you are dust, and to dust you shall return (Gen 3:19). And the spirit returns to God who gave it.

This answers the question the Preacher left open in 3:21, Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward? Now he says it: the spirit returns to God. Death is not extinction. Every person meets his Maker.

For those who belong to Christ, that return is a homecoming. Jesus died with this verse lived out: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit! (Luke 23:46). And Stephen, as the stones fell, prayed, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit (Acts 7:59). The spirit that returns to God can return in trust, into the hands of a Father, because Christ went that way first.

verseByVerse.quote: Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher; all is vanity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher; all is vanity.

The book comes full circle. These are almost the exact words of 1:2. The ESV notes that hebel appears three times in this verse. After everything, the verdict on life under the sun has not changed. It is breath.

But the reader has changed. The first time we heard these words, they sounded like despair. Now we have walked through the whole book. We have heard that God gives joy, that he makes everything beautiful in its time, that he has put eternity in the heart, that it will be well with those who fear him, and that the spirit returns to him. All is vanity now sounds less like the end of hope and more like a clearing of the ground. Everything under the sun is breath, so do not build your life on it. Build it on the one who is not under the sun.

And notice again the voice: says the Preacher. Someone is speaking about him, as in 1:2 and 7:27. That voice now takes over for the book's last words.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — The End of the Matter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Preacher was wise, taught the people, and arranged many proverbs with care, seeking words of delight and writing words of truth (vv. 9-10). The words of the wise are like goads, they are given by one Shepherd (v. 11). Beware of anything beyond these (v. 12). The end of the matter; all has been heard. Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man (v. 13). For God will bring every deed into judgment, with every secret thing, whether good or evil (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything under the sun is breath; the words of the one Shepherd are not, and they call us to fear God.

verseByVerse.quote: Besides being wise, the Preacher also taught the people knowledge, weighing and studying and arranging many proverbs with great care. The Preacher sought to find words of delight, and uprightly he wrote words of truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Besides being wise, the Preacher also taught the people knowledge, weighing and studying and arranging many proverbs with great care.

The frame narrator steps forward and tells us about the Preacher. He was not only wise himself; he taught others. And he did it with great care: weighing, studying, arranging. The ESV's rendering of his title in 1:1 had a note that he might be called "Collector". Here we see him at work, collecting and ordering sayings. Of Solomon it is written, He also spoke 3,000 proverbs (1 Kgs 4:32).

That matters for how we read the book. Ecclesiastes is not a man's raw diary of despair. It is a carefully crafted work of teaching. Every hard saying was weighed.

The Preacher sought to find words of delight, and uprightly he wrote words of truth.

Two aims: words of delight and words of truth. Beautiful and true. He wanted his words to be pleasing, well chosen, memorable, and he refused to make them pleasing at the cost of truth. Every teacher, preacher and parent needs both. Truth without delight is hard to hear; delight without truth is flattery. The words of Scripture are both: More to be desired are they than gold, sweeter also than honey (Ps 19:10), and your word is truth (John 17:17).

verseByVerse.quote: The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails firmly fixed are the collected sayings; they are given by one Shepherd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails firmly fixed are the collected sayings; they are given by one Shepherd.

Two pictures of what wise words do. A goad is a sharp stick used to prod oxen: it stings, it gets you moving, it keeps you in the furrow. Ecclesiastes has been goading us for twelve chapters, poking at our comfortable assumptions. And nails firmly fixed: once driven in, they hold. Wise sayings lodge in the mind and stay. Years later a person remembers Two are better than one or Cast your bread upon the waters.

The word of God does both. For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword (Heb 4:12): it goads. All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction (2 Tim 3:16): it fixes.

And the source: they are given by one Shepherd. Behind the Preacher's pen stands another. Many wise men wrote; one Shepherd gave the words. This is one of the clearest statements in the wisdom books that these sayings come from God. And the title is rich. The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want (Ps 23:1). God promised I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David (Ezek 34:23).

The book that began with the son of David, king in Jerusalem (1:1) ends by pointing to one Shepherd, and the New Testament shows us who he is. I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). The wisest son of David collected sayings; the greater Son of David is the Shepherd who gives them, the great shepherd of the sheep (Heb 13:20).

verseByVerse.quote: My son, beware of anything beyond these. Of making many books there is no end, and much study is a weariness of the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My son, beware of anything beyond these. Of making many books there is no end, and much study is a weariness of the flesh.

My son: the voice of a father, as in Proverbs. Beware of anything beyond these. The words given by the one Shepherd are enough. Do not go looking for wisdom that goes beyond them or contradicts them.

Of making many books there is no end. Every generation writes more books on the meaning of life, and the shelves never fill. Much study is a weariness of the flesh, as every student knows. This is not an attack on learning. The Preacher studied more than anyone. It is a warning against the endless search that never arrives, reading book after book hoping the next will finally explain everything. The Preacher tried that in chapter 1, and found that he who increases knowledge increases sorrow (1:18).

What the soul needs is not more books but the right one. In a world of endless information, the believer is freed from the treadmill of always searching. God has spoken, and in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son (Heb 1:2).

verseByVerse.quote: The end of the matter; all has been heard. Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The end of the matter; all has been heard. Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man.

Here is the conclusion of the whole book. All has been heard. The hard questions, the observations of injustice and death, the calls to joy: they have all been laid out. Now, the verdict.

Fear God. Not "understand everything". Not "find the scheme of things". The Preacher showed that we cannot. The answer to a world we cannot understand is to fear the God who does. The fear of God has been the quiet thread through the book (3:14; 5:7; 7:18; 8:12-13), and now it is the last word. It is where Proverbs began: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge (Prov 1:7). Wisdom begins and ends in the same place.

And keep his commandments. Fear that does not obey is not the fear of God. Moses said the same: what does the LORD your God require of you, but to fear the LORD your God, and to keep the commandments and statutes of the LORD (Deut 10:12-13). Jesus said, If you love me, you will keep my commandments (John 14:15), and John adds, his commandments are not burdensome (1 John 5:3).

For this is the whole duty of man. The ESV notes this may be rendered "the duty of all mankind". It is the whole of what a person is for, and it is for every person. Rich or poor, wise or foolish, young or old: this is what life under the sun is meant to be lived for. Everything else is breath. This is not.

After a lifetime of searching, the Preacher lands on something a child can understand. That is not a letdown. It is grace.

verseByVerse.quote: For God will bring every deed into judgment, with every secret thing, whether good or evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For God will bring every deed into judgment, with every secret thing, whether good or evil.

The final reason to fear God. Everything the Preacher saw go wrong under the sun, the oppression with no comforter, the wicked buried with honour, the righteous who perished, the poor wise man forgotten, will be brought before God. Every deed. Every secret thing. The ESV notes that the phrase may be rendered "into the judgment on every secret thing".

That is the answer to the book's great complaint. Under the sun, there is no justice and no final gain. But life is not lived only under the sun. God will judge, and nothing is too small or too hidden. Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed (Luke 12:2). The Lord will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart. Then each one will receive his commendation from God (1 Cor 4:5). So toil is not finally in vain; every good deed done in secret will be seen.

But the verse also leaves every reader exposed. Every secret thing, whether good or evil. If that is the last word, who can stand? The Preacher has already told us, there is not a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins (7:20).

That is why the book, for all its wisdom, cannot be the last book. It leaves us needing what the gospel gives. God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus (Rom 2:16), and the judge is the one who took the judgment. For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Cor 5:21). So Jesus can say, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life (John 5:24).

Ecclesiastes ends with judgment, and it is right to end there. Fear God, because he will judge. And then run to the Shepherd who laid down his life for the sheep, because in him There is therefore now no condemnation (Rom 8:1).

12.text: <sup>1</sup>Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come and the years draw near of which you will say, "I have no pleasure in them";<sup>2</sup>before the sun and the light and the moon and the stars are darkened and the clouds return after the rain,<sup>3</sup>in the day when the keepers of the house tremble, and the strong men are bent, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those who look through the windows are dimmed,<sup>4</sup>and the doors on the street are shut—when the sound of the grinding is low, and one rises up at the sound of a bird, and all the daughters of song are brought low—<sup>5</sup>they are afraid also of what is high, and terrors are in the way; the almond tree blossoms, the grasshopper drags itself along, and desire fails, because man is going to his eternal home, and the mourners go about the streets—<sup>6</sup>before the silver cord is snapped, or the golden bowl is broken, or the pitcher is shattered at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern,<sup>7</sup>and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it.<sup>8</sup>Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher; all is vanity.<sup>9</sup>Besides being wise, the Preacher also taught the people knowledge, weighing and studying and arranging many proverbs with great care.<sup>10</sup>The Preacher sought to find words of delight, and uprightly he wrote words of truth.<sup>11</sup>The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails firmly fixed are the collected sayings; they are given by one Shepherd.<sup>12</sup>My son, beware of anything beyond these. Of making many books there is no end, and much study is a weariness of the flesh.<sup>13</sup>The end of the matter; all has been heard. Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man.<sup>14</sup>For God will bring every deed into judgment, with every secret thing, whether good or evil.
12.overview:
The Preacher calls the young to remember their Creator before the evil days of old age come (v. 1). In a series of pictures he describes ageing: the lights darken and clouds return after rain (v. 2); the house of the body trembles, its grinders cease and its windows dim (vv. 3-4); fears multiply, the almond blossoms, desire fails, and man goes to his eternal home (v. 5). Then the silver cord snaps and the golden bowl breaks, and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it (vv. 6-7). Vanity of vanities, the book's opening verdict, returns (v. 8).

The narrator commends the Preacher, who taught the people and arranged proverbs with care, seeking words of delight and truth (vv. 9-10). The words of the wise are goads and fixed nails, given by one Shepherd; beyond them lies endless study (vv. 11-12).

The end of the matter; all has been heard. Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man. For God will bring every deed into judgment, with every secret thing, whether good or evil (vv. 13-14).
12.theology:
God is the Creator to be remembered from youth onward (v. 1). At death the body returns to dust and the spirit to God (v. 7; Gen 2:7; 3:19), answering the open question of 3:21; for believers that return is into a Father's hands (Luke 23:46; Acts 7:59; 2 Cor 5:1).

The words of the wise are given by one Shepherd (v. 11): Scripture is God's word, sufficient and final (v. 12; 2 Tim 3:16; Heb 1:2), and the Shepherd is revealed as Christ (John 10:11; Heb 13:20).

The whole duty of every person is to fear God and keep his commandments (v. 13; Prov 1:7; Deut 10:12-13). God will judge every deed and secret thing (v. 14; Rom 2:16; 1 Cor 4:5), and since none is righteous (7:20), the only refuge is Christ, in whom there is no condemnation (John 5:24; Rom 8:1; 2 Cor 5:21).
12.examples:
Giving your youth to God rather than your leftovers.

Caring for an ageing parent and recognising every line of verses 3-5.

A golden lamp falling when its cord snaps.

A goad in the ox's side and a nail driven home.

The shelf of books on the meaning of life that never fills.

Every secret thing brought to light, and the Shepherd who took the judgment.
